paragraphs.text: By naming him "the Word," the evangelist presents him as the Creator of all things. Since, as a rule, all making depends on reason, there was no other way to show that he is the maker of all things [?] (for art is a productive habit joined to unerring reason). And the Son of God, being nothing other than the craftsman of wisdom and art, is fittingly called the Word. For he is not some other being, distinct from the Word, who makes things through the Word; he himself is the one who makes, being God the Word. Then, since this Word, who is God in essence and is for that very reason the Son of God, became man for the salvation of human beings, the Word was called "flesh." And since some who have fallen from the right faith suppose that he has existed only from the time when he came forth from the Virgin, having become man, the Theologian writes, most rightly against such people, "In the beginning was the Word." He uses his verbs fittingly, signifying the flesh by "became" and his Godhead by "was." It would indeed have been more proper to say "is" of God the Word; but since he was showing the existence of the Word in contrast to the incarnation, which took place at a particular time, the evangelist used "was" instead of "is." Yet with eternal things we must not take verbs in their strict senses. When the things they signify have an existence measured out by time, "was" indicates what no longer is, and likewise "is" indicates what exists now, and "will be" what is going to exist. But since the Word of God is eternal, being God, the verbs used of him must not be taken as also signifying time, because what they signify is not subject to time. The meaning can be traced from the Theologian's own words. Right at the start of his composition he writes, "In the beginning was the Word": for he was in the beginning, making heaven and earth. If "all things came into being through him," and heaven and earth are among all things, then when they were brought into being he was their Creator. Then, since he did not say that the Word was in the beginning of some particular thing, it must be taken universally, so that the meaning is this: in the beginning of the angels, and in the beginning of the archangels, was the Word; in short, in the beginning of creatures visible and invisible was the Word, being both the beginning and the maker of them all. For in Christ "all things were created," both "those in the heavens and those on earth, things visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities; all things were created through him and for him; and he is before all things, and in him all things hold together; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead." For if all things hold together in him, and he is before them, being their beginning as the cause of their existence, it follows that we must say he was there when all things were brought into being. How could he, being their Creator, not have been before them and in the beginning of their existence? Then, since he had said that he was in the beginning, he needed to show how, and with whom, he was when he was to make things. That is why he added to "In the beginning was the Word" the words "and the Word was with God." For when he came to us, when he was born of the Virgin, he had been sent by the Father; therefore

he also "dwelt among us" and received the very name "God with us." But when he created, since he did not bring all things into being as a man sent by the Father, he was both with God and was God. The Son of God is also called Wisdom, created as the beginning of God's ways, according to the text of Proverbs, because the Wisdom of God, being with him whose Wisdom it is, had no relation to anything else; but, God being well pleased, he willed that the creatures should come into being. So this Wisdom willed to take on a creative relation to the things that were to be, and that is what is meant by its having been created as the beginning of God's ways: the ways along which he goes forth, bringing beings into existence, ordering them, providing for them, doing them good, and bestowing grace, in this Wisdom that was created. They say, then, that the Word is the beginning, not as being different from Wisdom in essence but in concept and relation, so that the one and the same existence which the Scriptures now call [?] according to essence is Wisdom insofar as it belongs properly to God, and is the creative Word insofar as it has turned, so to speak, toward the things it creates. The Son of God is called the Word not only here; one can cite passages not only from the New Testament but also from the Old: "By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm," and "He sent out his word and healed them." And Luke says, "Just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the word handed them down to us."

What has come into being in him, that is, in the Word, was life. Just as God brought all things into existence, so the things whose nature it is to live were to be made alive by sharing in him. That is why it is fittingly said: "And the life was the light of men." We must not listen to those who have concluded from this phrase that the Word is a created being. What has come into being is not itself life. But this life did not come upon him from outside, for life came into being in him. Created beings could not possess him, who is life by essence, in the way that he is with the Father. For it is said to God: "With you is the fountain of life." This life is with the Father, but it does not give life to him, for the Father does not live by sharing in life. Rather, God, being life, begets life, just as, being wise, he begets wisdom, and being powerful, he begets power. This life, wishing to benefit rational beings, took on a relation toward them, since they received it by way of participation in order to live. And this must be said not only of the life they share in common but also of the life of virtue, by which one comes to live well. This is shown at any rate by the very wording, for it says: "And the life was the light of men." That this is the meaning here can also be confirmed from another point. The Son and Word of God, being God the Word, is with God, as has just been said. Yet he also comes to be with human beings, as far as they are able to receive his presence. For it is said: "The word of the Lord came to Hosea," and "The word of the Lord came to Jeremiah," and in general: "He called them gods to whom the word of God came." So just as he is the Word with God but comes to be with created beings, so, being life, he is with the Father and gives life to those he visits. A life-giving relation comes to be in him, in harmony with the things that are made alive. But besides giving life, this life also produces knowledge of the truth, enlightening the minds of those who receive it, and so it is also called the light of men. And since it is the light of men, it clearly also enlightens the higher rational beings. For if it is the light of the lesser rational beings, it is much more the light of those that surpass them.

The divine light dissolves all darkness, ignorance and wickedness that exists. That is why, shining in such darkness, it is not overcome by it. This light is the wisdom and righteousness of God. As wisdom, it dissolves the ignorance of the mind; as righteousness, it directs the steps of the soul. This is what its shining in the darkness means: nothing prevents it from sending out its own rays to the person who is being enlightened. Therefore it is not overcome by the darkness, since the darkness is dissolved and vanishes at its presence. The darkness fails to overcome the light not while it still exists and is active, but by being dissolved and no longer existing. For example, when Paul did not know Christ, he persecuted him, driven to this by the ignorance in him, which we have said is darkness. But when the light it was persecuting shone out its own rays, the darkness was dissolved, and so it could not overcome the light it was persecuting. In the same way the robber who repented [?], blinded by the darkness just mentioned, was persecuting the light. But the darkness in the robber was dissolved, and so it does not overcome the light. To put the idea more clearly: truth is light. When falsehood and every kind of deceit, which is to say darkness, pursues the light, it is dissolved and vanishes as it comes near what it is pursuing. For when the truth appears, falsehood and deceit are dissolved. And here is the paradox: while it is far away, the darkness pursues the light, but when it comes near enough to overtake it, it vanishes. For as long as falsehood stands apart from the truth, it prevails and is at work in a person, so that it drives the truth from the mind. But when it comes near the truth, it is shown not to exist at all. That is why God, though he could have prevented it, necessarily allowed wickedness to exist, so that the greatness of virtue might be displayed.

[He is called a man] not so much because of the common definition of a human being as because he is by nature made in the image of God and for likeness to God. It should be noted that "there was" (literally "came to be") does not always refer to being brought into existence. Here "came to be" refers to "sent from God," so that the statement means: "He came, sent from God, for testimony." And if these things said about John are correct, how much more so are the things written or said about the Son of God, as one who is said or written about and comes to be [?].

That all might believe. That is, as far as it depended on him, even if not all believed. If not everyone received the light that comes from the sun, no one would say on that account that the sun does not rise for the purpose of giving light to all. For the purpose of the one who sent him was that all should believe.

He was not the light. That is, not the divine light. Some had supposed, because of the distinctions he possessed, that he himself was the Christ. So the evangelist says this in order to tear such an error out by the roots. For even if John is a light, he is not that light of which the saints say to God: "In your light we shall see light." So although John was a light, in the sense of what was said to the disciples, "You are the light of the world," he was not that true light. "True light" is said not in contrast with falsehood but to distinguish it from an image. Truth and what is true are sometimes contrasted with falsehood and deceit, and sometimes with an image and imitation. We may take the light of the senses, and especially the sun, as the light that is an image, and the intelligible light as the true light, or rather the light that enlightens intelligible beings, the holy powers. I think this is what Scripture means when it says: "Every good gift and every perfect present is from above, coming down from the Father of lights." For the divine light was "the true light, which enlightens every person coming into the world." But since "coming into the world" is ambiguous, and can refer either to the light or to the person, it must be interpreted both ways. First, we should take it to mean the light that enlightens every person, coming at the time of his sojourn among us, while the person is in the world. In this sense, as has been said, it is the light that comes into the world to enlighten humanity. Second, the true light enlightens every person who comes into the world.

Not everyone turned away from him, for many of them accepted him, especially the apostles. So the evangelist adds: "But as many as received him obtained power to become children of God." Those who are being introduced to the faith, and perhaps also those who have made progress, have the power to become children of God. For now they have received the power, and they will become children when they are made perfect in virtue, faith and knowledge. He shows the reason they had this power by writing that it was given to those who believed in his name, that is, the name of the light. Believing in the name of the light is not the same as believing in the light. So power, that is, a fitness to become children, is given to those who believe in his name. But if through progress they pass from believing in his name to believing in him, they would be children of God no longer potentially but actually. Some assent to the light with a simpler understanding that is not fully worked out, and they believe in his name. Others come to him with scientific demonstration and a well-articulated understanding, and they believe in him and call upon him. That is why Jesus, after his disciples had made great progress, says: "Since you believe in God, believe also in me." This means: "It is time for you to move on from believing in my name, so that you may believe in me and in the Father." Indeed, after explaining the highest theology to them, he added, as if speaking to all: "Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?"

Those born of God were born of God by believing that Jesus is the Christ and by doing righteousness. They are not subject to birth from blood, that is, they do not have their origin from material things. Indeed, when Peter believed that the Christ is the Son of the living God, the Savior said to him: "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, for flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father in heaven." Consider also whether, on another reading, someone can be a son of blood who thinks he is devout and a son of God because he offers the material sacrifices prescribed by the law. Such people think they please God through slaughter and the shedding of blood. Doing this was blameless in earlier times, but it is no longer so for us, because the blood of Jesus, given for us, is enough for justification. Those who do everything in order to appear righteous to people are subject to the will of the flesh and to birth from a man. They set out to please by the will of the flesh, circumcising the flesh and wanting to practice Judaism outwardly, while neglecting the heart and the Judaism that is in secret. Those who abstain from vice and take up virtue on the grounds of human philosophy have their birth from the will of a man. Above all these, then, is the one who has been born of God by believing in him after first believing in his name.

"As of the only-begotten from the Father" leads us to understand that the Son is from the essence of the Father. None of the creatures is from the Father; each has its being from God through the Word. If other things also had their existence from the Father, the word "only-begotten" would have been used in vain, since there would be many that have their being from the Father. But he is said to be the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth, and he is not something other than the things of which he is said to be full. For the only-begotten himself says of himself: "I am the truth." What is filled by truth would be something that receives truth, but truth does not receive truth, since it actually is what it is said to be. The same could be said about grace. It is not strange to say such things about the only-begotten, since similar things are recorded about the Father. He himself says of himself in the prophet: "I am full." It is likely that this phrase was also used because of what will be observed about the time before the Savior's coming. The law given through Moses punished sinners and pardoned no one for anything done in transgression of it. Moreover, this law handed down the rites of mysteries through images and shadow-sketches, leading by the hand and preparing those who were guided by them for the teaching of Christ. That is why the law is also called a tutor leading to Christ. The Savior, then, came not to punish those who had sinned but to grant forgiveness for what they had done. He came to bring the teaching to its completion and to give the knowledge of the truth in place of images, revealing the truth himself, or rather being himself the truth. So he fittingly appeared full of grace and truth to those who beheld him. If he had shown grace to some and not to others, he would not have been full of grace. In the same way, if he had brought one part of the shadow to an end but not another, he would not have been full of truth. But in fact he did away with every shadow and image, and he grants forgiveness of all sins to those who flee to him in repentance. Therefore he is full of truth and grace.

Cried out [?]. Not in the sound of his voice but in the intensity of his thought. Whoever proclaims the great doctrines rightly utters them loudly, in thought. "First" should be understood in place of [?]. In any case, what he means is this: Jesus, who is before me and prior to me, came after me and later than me, not to remain behind me but to come to be ahead of me. Jesus' coming after John should be understood in terms of the time of birth, for John was conceived six months before Jesus. In this way Jesus, who came after him, came to be ahead of him, since he was shown to be God and John's creator. It could also be put this way: every learner will seem [?] to his teacher, and in this sense he is said to walk behind him. Now the Savior also came to John while he was baptizing, in order to be baptized. In being baptized by John, he is said to come after the baptizer. But in having been sanctified and given testimony by the Father, he came to be ahead of the baptizer and was shown to be more honorable than him and superior to him. It is also well said that "he has come to be ahead of me," since his existence comes before his having come to be. Note also how precisely this is said. It is not written, "He who is after me"; how could such a one be before him [?]? But it is not impossible for the one who is first to come after. It could also be explained in another way. "Because," he says, "from his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace." Here again he gives the reason why the one who is first came to be ahead of him, adding: "Because from his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace." How could the one who fills not be ahead in pre-eminence, and first among those who are filled? If he himself perfects those who come to holiness and fills them with virtue and wisdom, how could he not be first and pre-eminent over them? Pay attention to the precision of what is written. It does not say that we received "his fullness," but that "from his fullness we have all received." Those who share in holiness and in the knowledge of truth in this life know in part and prophesy in part. They have this from his fullness, but they do not have his fullness itself. They may have it in the [?] life of the ages to come, as the apostle says: "When the perfect comes, what is in part will be done away." The words in John's catholic epistle agree with this: "It has not yet been revealed what we shall be; but we know that when it is revealed we shall be like him, for we shall see him as he is." That is, we shall see him as far as created beings can know God, for it is not possible to grasp God as he himself is. Even so, we shall have something more than our present state, if we no longer know in part but, stripped of ignorance, encounter the purest truth and see him as far as possible. So John says of Jesus, "He has come to be ahead of me," because John had received from his fullness. And the fact that not just one but all the saints receive from the fullness of Jesus shows the superiority of the one who fills and perfects them. For if all the saints were filled not from the whole fullness but from some part of it, those who receive from the fullness will be seen to fall far short of the one who supplied it to them.

Part of virtue we have from within, from ourselves, and we acquire it by choice; the other part comes from God. Having believed in the Savior and his Father, as far as was possible by what is in our power, we still need to ask for what comes from God. So Jesus' disciples say to him: "Increase our faith." The word "increase" (literally "add") shows that they were asking for faith given by God in addition to the faith they had by choice. Indeed, Paul writes that the gifts of the Spirit are given "according to the proportion of faith," that is, the faith present in us through what is in our power. "To another," he says, "is given faith by the same Spirit." If faith is given to someone in proportion to the faith he already has, it is clear that faith sent by God comes to faith achieved by our own power. What has been said about faith must also be said about the other virtues. Virtue is a grace that makes its possessor gracious. So when we achieve it by choice, then what comes from God arrives. This is what is meant by God giving grace for grace.

The law was given through Moses, but not by him. It was given by God, for the law is God's, as it is written: "The law of the Lord is blameless, turning souls back." Though the law is given through Moses, "grace and truth came through Jesus Christ." Grace, through the forgiveness of sins, prevents the punishment that the law brings upon sinners, and truth goes beyond the shadows and the types. Consider also what is about to be said. The law and the prophets lasted until John, so that he became the end of the old scripture, and after it the Savior's coming took place. So it is very fittingly said: "He who comes after me has come to be ahead of me." Since the Savior's descent was announced beforehand by the law and the prophets, when he came he is said to have come after. But although he came after, he nevertheless came to be ahead, since he fulfilled the law and the prophets by revealing what was divine in them. He was shown to be the cause of all that inspired scripture, which lasted until John the Baptist.

Seeing is of two kinds, sensory and intellectual. The first perceives bodies, the second incorporeal things. That is why we call the objects of the mind, the things the mind contemplates, invisible. This is not because they are not seen, but because they are not by nature such as to be seen. No body is invisible, even if it is sometimes out of sight and not seen. "Invisible" does not mean "not seen"; it means not naturally able to be seen. So "not seen" and "invisible" are not interchangeable. Not being seen follows from being invisible [?]. But many bodies, though visible, are not seen, either because they are covered or because they are not where the viewer is. Since this distinction is correct, the statement must be taken as referring to the invisible. Not even the highest powers see God, not because of their own weakness but because God is incorporeal. Nor is he visible to the mind without qualification, but only to a mind freed from all ignorance, wickedness and matter. "Blessed," it says, "are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." By "heart" it means the mind. Whoever has become pure in the way described and has been perfected in virtue encounters God as far as that is attainable. This being so, the mind that is still subject to becoming, and therefore to time, does not see God as [?]. So he did not simply say, "No one has seen God," but added "ever," which indicates something temporal. The statement thus means: for as long as "ever" can be said, as indicating some underlying state, the mind is sold into material life. Therefore it cannot see God by an act of understanding. We understand him dimly, as far as possible, from the concepts we hold about him in theology. But God himself understands himself not through anything of this kind but through his intimacy with himself, since he himself is both the understanding and what is understood. That is why only the Son knows him, being understood by the Father and understanding the Father.

The Father's bosom is mentioned because he is the only-begotten God and Son. Everything concerning the Godhead is beyond naming, and it is made known to us as human beings through human words. So the evangelist fittingly used things whose meaning we know to signify his intimacy with the Father, writing: "who is in the bosom of the Father." It is written that all who are saved and receive God's promises will be in the bosom of Abraham. This means nothing other than that Abraham is called the father of the faithful. In the same way the Son of God is said to be in the bosom of the one who begot him. Just as faithful people come to be in the bosom of faithful Abraham, so the Son, being the Son, is in the bosom of the Father. The Father's bosom must be understood in the same way as the other things said of God in human terms. And when prophets, patriarchs or angels are said to have seen God, divine Scripture does not contradict itself. For no one sees God by applying his own understanding, in the way that we are said to see visible things by directing our sight at them. Yet God is seen by those to whom he decides to be seen, revealing himself. If anyone saw God by his own power, he would behold him, so to speak, as he is and in all his greatness. But since a person does not see by himself, and it is God who shows himself, God offers himself to be understood as far as is possible for created beings. As the Savior also says: "And I will manifest myself to him." He did not say, "He will see me," but "I will manifest myself to him." And this is * * *

The forerunner stands in relation to different aspects of the Savior. He is the prophet of God. He is the lamp of the light, giving early light to those in the night of ignorance and training the eye of the soul in advance, so that it can run toward the great light. [[He is the morning star, the herald of the sun, signaling the arrival of the day that is about to dawn upon us.]] He is the voice of the Word, for a voice must come before a word. That is why he says: "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness." By the one crying he means the Word, and by the wilderness the soul that is ignorant of divine teaching. For how is that soul not a wilderness, deprived as it is of God's Word and of the voice that makes him known? The task of the voice is to make clear what is meant, so that people can grasp the Word being revealed without confusion. What does the voice of the one crying command the wilderness? "Make straight," it says, "the way of the Lord." The wilderness stands for all who do not know the one who comes after the voice. The one who goes ahead of a king commands those to whom the king is coming to make the way straight. In the same way, John commands that the way of those coming to the teaching of the Word be made straight. [[So John goes ahead of the Word. For just as a voice runs ahead of a word, so John, as the voice, runs ahead of Christ, who is the Word.]]

What does John mean by saying, "Among you stands one whom you do not know," when Jesus was not yet there at the time? For in what follows it says, "The next day he sees Jesus coming toward him," which shows that he was not there when John, bearing witness about the light, said, "Among you stands." John knew that he was also God the Word, and the Word is present to every rational being. Some suppose that the thinking faculty, which some call the ruling faculty, lies at our very centre. The Word by which we are rational is there, and it is the same as the image of God according to which man was made in God's image. So, to show that the Word of God is the one who was about to come to be baptized by him, John says, "Among you stands" one unknown to you. And he is unknown to you for this reason: you have him in your midst and ought to do what is fitting, yet you keep him idle within you and, so to speak, inactive, doing and thinking nothing rationally. Having said this about the essence of the Word, he next adds what concerns his coming, saying, "He who comes after me", that is, after the law and the prophets, for I am their symbol and their end. He comes after me fulfilling everything that was prophesied about him, since the one who is prophesied comes after the things proclaimed beforehand. "And among you he stands," as we have already explained, "the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie." You should understand "the strap of the sandal" in this way. What the Word of God administers for the sake of human beings he does not carry out with naked divinity. He took the form of a servant, so that his progress in carrying out the economy is veiled. This is said of him in the Psalms too: "He bowed the heavens and came down, and thick darkness was under his feet." [[There is something dark about his progress, because it is obscure.]] So the strap of his sandal, that is, of the darkness about his feet, is the principle of incomprehensibility, which binds the sandal tight and holds it about his feet. To untie the strap would therefore be to make clear and set out in reason how God took up a body, covering and hiding the power by which he advances to the economy. Since no human being can demonstrate the manner of the union, it is fitting that he who was more than a prophet, than whom no one born of women is greater, confesses that he is not able to untie the strap of his sandal.

It is also well said, "who takes away the sin," and not "who took away" or "who will take away." For he is always at work taking away the sin of those who take refuge in him. From this we show that he took it away, takes it away and will take it away, the taking away applying to every time.

And I did not know him. "I who teach," he says, "did not say these things about Christ by my own nature or from the common understanding of human beings. I did not know him. I spoke the testimonies about him because the Holy Spirit and the Father revealed them to me. I was sent to bear witness about the light, and I received the beginning of knowledge of the one I bear witness to when I was sent." But the "not knowing" must also be approached in another way [?]. When he says of the Savior, "And I did not know him," he is not saying anything contrary to what he testified about him. The phrase shows that he did not know him before, but now knows that this is the one, because God revealed it to him. This is clear from what is said immediately afterward. For John himself says again that he beheld the Spirit coming down upon the Lord in the form of a dove. "And I did not know him," he says, "but the one who sent me to baptize with water said to me, 'He on whom you see the Spirit descending, this is my Son.' And I have seen and have testified." Even before the descent of the Spirit he knew him as the lamb, as the man, as the Prophet, as the Christ and as the true light. Yet he still lacked the knowledge that he was the Son of God and the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit, and he gained this when the sign he had been given was seen. That being so, we must ask how John says he beheld the Spirit. It is not right to think that the Spirit, whose existence is intelligible, is seen by the senses. So we will take up the problem in general terms and examine, together with this passage, the things said in a similar way in the prophecies. For many of the prophets, and in short many of the holy men, are recorded as having beheld visions and sights. Elsewhere too "seeing" and "beholding" have been divided into two kinds, sense perception and understanding. It is impossible that the holy men saw God with the senses, or indeed the Trinity at all, or the things beneath it that have intelligible existence. It remains, then, that they beheld the visions by understanding, not as these visions have substance in themselves, but as they can be seen through some analogy. Indeed, the Holy Spirit has no shape or form or appearance of any kind, yet John receives a conception of him as a dove. The Holy Spirit does not move from place to place, yet John sees a descent from heaven onto Jesus as he is baptized. And what comes next shows that none of these things was perceived by the senses: "He on whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining on him." One can see the descent of something with the senses when it happens to be a body. † But it is not by sight but by understanding that one sees that what has descended [remains] on the one upon whom it descended; sense perception does not grasp things that remain in such a way as to confirm this vision. [?] We must also argue from a further proof. The other evangelists say that John saw the Spirit descend upon the Son, and that he also saw the heavens opened or torn. But no one can see an opening or tearing of the heavens with the senses, since one cannot see this even in denser bodies, I mean water and air, and let us add ether, if it is something other than the heavens. When things pass through continuous bodies that are not hard, they pass through them without the opening and passage being made for them from anywhere else. The things passing through open these bodies themselves, and the bodies close up again once they have passed through. At any rate, divisions in water cannot be seen unless a more solid body is thrust into it. If so, an opening of the heavens could not fall under sight, since the Holy Spirit who came down from there is not a body either. So the Baptist beheld these things too intelligibly. We must also note that the Holy Spirit remained on Jesus alone. If, having descended, it had remained on someone else too, it would not have been a sign pointing out the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit. This must be shown as follows. The Holy Spirit dwells in undefiled and pure souls and cannot bear to be where there is sin. "For the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit and will withdraw from foolish thoughts." And David, when he had fallen into a certain sin, entreated God, saying, "Do not take your Holy Spirit from me." Since Jesus alone committed no sin, and no deceit was in his mouth (for of him alone it is said, "him who knew no sin"), it was fitting that the Holy Spirit descended upon him and remained. All these things, I mean the Spirit's coming down from heaven upon Jesus and remaining on him, were written for the sake of the economy. They are not a historical narrative but an intelligible contemplation, as has already been said. For the Holy Spirit cannot be separated from the Son. Neither the Son nor the Father is in a place, such that the Holy Spirit would have to move from place to place and pass from the Father to the Son. In general, what concerns the Godhead should be taken intelligibly, even when it is spoken of in human terms, such as standing, sitting and going up [[and whatever else of the kind is written about the Godhead]].

It is worth asking how Andrew here immediately finds his own brother Peter on the second day after Jesus' baptism, while elsewhere, according to Matthew, Jesus finds Peter and his brother Andrew many days after the baptism. Probably Andrew first brought Peter to Jesus, and Peter received a little benefit from the teacher. Then, after his brother had been helped, they withdrew to attend to their own affairs. After this first call, Jesus called them to follow him continually, giving them the power to fish for people through the teaching he provided them. "Come," he says, "and see." Perhaps by "Come" he summons them to the active life, and by "See" he indicates that those who wish it will certainly gain the contemplation that follows the right performance of actions, and that it comes as they persevere in them.

He said that he would be called Peter, a name taken from the rock, which is Christ. Just as one is wise from wisdom and holy from holiness, so too Peter from the rock * *. This is shown by what the Savior said to the one who was given this name: "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church."

The words "The next day he wanted to go out into Galilee" are ambiguous: they can mean that it was Andrew who went out, or that it was Jesus. But the statement seems rather to be about Andrew, who went out into Galilee and found Philip. To this Philip, whom Andrew had found, Jesus says, "Follow me." To follow Jesus is to follow reason, wisdom and righteousness, acting and thinking rightly. In Greek, Bethsaida is translated "House of hunters." To such people Jesus said, "Come after me, and I will make you fishers of people." Concerning such hunters, sent as though from God, there is a prophecy in Jeremiah, spoken in the person of God, which runs: "And behold, I am sending you many hunters, who will hunt you."
He does not mean that the prophets wrote that Jesus would be the son of Joseph from Nazareth. He means that we have found this man to be the one of whom Moses in the law, and the prophets, spoke.

"Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" Either he says this in doubt: can so great a good come from Nazareth? Or he says it with confidence: the one who has been found really is from Nazareth, and truly he is good. Philip answers him, "Come and see" the Jesus who has been found, wishing to convince him by sight rather than by hearsay about the one who has been found.

…race, you are king.> For to see into the heart and to know who has guile in himself and who does not belongs to the Son of God, and not to one of the many sons, but to the Only-begotten, who is king of the chosen race. And this is Jesus; therefore he was also the Son of God.

You saw me back when I was under the fig tree, before I was called by Philip. Hearing this, Jesus says: “Because I told you that I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe?” You will see greater things than these. Now that the literal sense has been clarified [?], we must speak of the allegorical sense. By following Jesus, who is the Word of God and the Wisdom of God, Philip became a hunter of the souls that God gives to those able to benefit them. For Nathanael is interpreted >“gift of the Lord.”< To this disciple who had been given to him he does not at once impart the things concerning the divinity of the Son of God, but speaks of his becoming man: “He whom all of us Hebrews alike read of in the writings of Moses and the prophets as the one who is to come, we have found: Jesus, born of the virgin without the sowing of a man's seed, who is called the son of Joseph, the man betrothed to Mary, and whose origin, as to place, is from Nazareth.” For Nazareth is the virgin's town. Having received this from Philip, who had now become his teacher, the disciple Nathanael says to the one who taught him: “If what has been found is from Nazareth, is it any good?” At once Philip, calling him to see the matter with his own eyes, says to him: “Come and see,” not wishing his disciple to remain forever a hearer of words but to become a beholder of the truth, hastening on to contemplation after hearing the words. Jesus, seeing Nathanael coming not only by walking but also by advancing toward contemplation, bears witness about him as one so eager [?] for the understanding of the truth, and says to those with him: “Do you see this man coming? He is an Israelite not only outwardly and according to the flesh, but also according to spirit and understanding. For he has a mind that sees God; he is truly an Israelite and not falsely so called, since, being free of all guile, he is a friend of the truth.”

On the third day after Jesus had been baptized, there was a wedding at Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there, and Jesus himself was invited along with his disciples. For since Jesus is the maker of man and woman, he does not decline an invitation to a wedding, since he is himself the one who, after forming Eve, brought her to Adam. That is why in the gospel too he says about the union: “What God has joined together, let no man separate.” Let the heretics who reject marriage, then, be put to shame, since Jesus is invited to a wedding and his mother is there. The Manichaeans too must be refuted, who say that Mary was not the mother of Jesus, since the evangelist testifies that Jesus had a mother.]

The evangelist's precision can be seen from this narrative as well. Since he knew that the willfully malicious knaves among the Jews were ready to slander the mighty works of Jesus, he presents Jesus giving orders about drawing the water not to his own disciples but to the servants at the feast. For if Jesus' disciples had drawn the water, the slanderers would have said: “They filled the jars with wine and pretended to have filled them with water.” In keeping with this line of thought stands also the phrase “They filled the jars up to the brim”]]; and so as to leave no pretext for sophistry—as though, the jars not having been filled with water, wine had been added—it was made plain [?] that the whole had come from water]].

“They believed” is said in place of >“They were confirmed.”< For the most part he uses “faith” rather in the sense of confirmation. To these, then, he manifested his glory all the more. For to change a substance belongs to the Creator, not to a creature. Water becoming wine is not simply a change of quality but of substance.

And after this he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother and his brothers and his disciples. Many ask about the brothers of Jesus, how he came to have them, since Mary remained a virgin until her death.]] He had no brothers by nature, for the virgin bore no other child, nor was he himself from Joseph. So they were called his brothers by law, being sons of Joseph by a wife who had died earlier; and since Mary, by the betrothal agreement, was called his wife. [[For this is what the law of Moses teaches, which imposes the penalty for adultery on anyone who lies with a betrothed virgin; for it adds: “Because he humbled his neighbor's wife, he shall die.” If, then, the law calls the virgin pledged to Joseph his wife]], in keeping with such an ordinance the sons of Joseph are called the brothers of Jesus, even though he himself was not from Joseph.
