Of the three public feasts handed down to the Hebrews by the great hierophant Moses, one was the feast called Passover, which surpassed the other two in that it signified the deliverance from Egypt and the passage to the holy land. For this festival, at any rate, the whole Jewish nation hurried to Jerusalem from all the cities and villages, for the law had prescribed that the Passover be sacrificed in this city alone. The three feasts were named after God, who had instituted them by law. But since the Jews no longer kept the feasts according to the ordinance but according to their own appetites and pleasures, the evangelist calls it not the Passover of God but the Passover of the Jews. For they no longer came to Jerusalem for the sake of worship but for the sake of luxury. Everything for feasting was brought there from all the surrounding places and was sold in the house of God; for the evangelist said that oxen and sheep and doves were sold there as in some marketplace. And since it happened that those coming to the feast did not bring so much silver with them, certain money-changers hit upon the idea of setting up tables there and changing money, that is, lending, taking gold from those who needed silver—people who had come to get drunk and live in luxury rather than to keep the feast. So while the whole Jewish nation was there, given over to drunkenness, Jesus entered the house of God and drove them all out of it, holding nothing but a whip made of cords. This could not have been accomplished if he had been an ordinary man † and had undertaken to do it [?]; for he drove out of the house not only the rest of the crowd but even those who were selling what was needed for the feasting. Let no one think that this is a lesser thing than his other miracles. For without divine power it would not have been possible for one man to drive out so great a crowd, especially when they were enraged and thirsting for his blood. Indeed, the Jews themselves, astounded at what he had dared, say to him in what follows: “What sign do you show us for doing these things?” As if to say: How great are you in power, and what kind of piety are you able to perform, that you do such things, daring by yourself to drive out an entire, populous nation?]

They believed, not in him, but in his name. These people did not have firm or complete knowledge (they were spoken of earlier as well), but a knowledge that could very easily fall away. That is why he did not entrust himself to them: he knew all things, not on the surface, but from the depths of the mind. Even a mere human being can know people from their deeds and words. But Jesus, who was not a mere man but God made man, knows all things and grasps what is hidden in the mind. For it is said of God alone: "He who knows hidden things, and knows all things before they come to be." And since Jesus, being God, knows what is hidden in the heart, he has no need to receive testimony from anyone, for he knows what is in a person. It does not say simply that he knows people, but that he knows what is in a person. And since he knew that they would not hold on to the faith they had in his name, he did not entrust himself to them. They had believed because of signs, not because they understood anything about God. So they could quickly fall away, deceived by themselves or by others who would use clever arguments [?] to persuade them that perhaps the signs had not really happened, or had not happened rightly. But whoever believes in him with an understanding that comes from God is not easily deceived.

Nicodemus must also be counted among the many who had believed in the name of Jesus. He was one of the Pharisees and a ruler of the Jews. He certainly thought that Jesus was a teacher who had God with him, but not that he was God, as his own words show. He said, "You have come from God as a teacher," and then, as if to support what he knew about the teacher, he added: "For no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him." So the evangelist fittingly recorded that he came at night. He came at a time when he would escape the notice of the many Pharisees, of whom he was one. Or rather, and this cannot be disputed, he came at night because he was ignorant of the God he was approaching and had not yet been enlightened. The sun of righteousness had not yet risen for him, the sun that makes the spiritual day. Abraham longed for that day and prepared himself to see it, and when he saw it he rejoiced. The Pharisees are people who belong to the leading order and party in Judaism. They profess a strenuous way of life and an exact keeping of the law and the prophets. As a result they are for the most part bold and arrogant, and this is also how they got their name. For among the Hebrews "Phares" [?]. Since these people separate themselves from the whole Jewish nation, as if they surpassed it in wisdom and way of life, they want to be named after "Phares."

The word "anew" (anōthen) sometimes means from the [?] and [?], as in "He who comes from above is above all," and sometimes means [?], as in "to which you wish to be enslaved over again," that is, [?]. The birth from above that the Savior teaches about comes from taking up virtue and keeping his commandments. He says to the disciples: "Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may become sons of your Father in heaven." Nicodemus answered these words mistakenly. Even so, what he said contains some truth, though he himself did not understand it. Truly, no one who stays merely human, growing old in the human condition, can receive the birth that is according to the Spirit and from above. No one who remains unjust and unbelieving can be born according to righteousness and faith. In the same way, no one who remains in human things and grows old in them can receive the birth that makes new. That is why the teacher of truth writes to those eager to come to the divine birth that they should put off the old self with its deeds. When this has been cast off, they are to put on the new self, "created according to God in righteousness." As one born from above, that new self will then walk in newness of life. Jesus was urging his disciples toward this birth when he said: "Unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven." Notice how precise this saying is too. Children do not retaliate against those who have wronged them. They do not grieve at losing pleasant things, and they do not cling steadily even to those who are kind to them. He wants us, then, to be by disposition what children happen to be by age. Children are like this without reasoning about it. But those who become like them at Jesus' command strive to be found this way by reason and by the best of habits. So even though Nicodemus spoke these words in ignorance, there was still a truth in them that he did not know.

Explaining how it is possible "to be born from above," the Savior says: [?]. Since the goal set before us is to enter the kingdom of God, and no one can reach it without being born of water and the Spirit, being born from above goes together with being born of water and the Spirit. A person is born of the Spirit when he is formed according to the Spirit and becomes holy and spiritual through it. And since whoever enters the kingdom of God is born not of the Spirit alone but also of water, we should next search out something in Scripture about the water. Consider whether the water differs from the Spirit only in concept and not in substance. Later on the Savior says: "Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from within him. He said this about the Spirit, which those who believed in him were to receive." If this is said about the Spirit, as living water flowing like rivers out of the believer, then the water will differ from the Spirit only in concept. A person is born of the Savior and becomes wise from Wisdom. In the same way he is born of the Spirit and becomes holy and spiritual. And when he is cleansed by the water and watered so that he bears fruit, he is born of water and the Spirit. But someone else will say that "water" here means the teaching that cleanses the soul, which also helps a person to be born from above. The psalmist spoke to God about this cleansing, which comes through divine instruction: "You will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow." And [?] says to the multitude of Israel: "Wash your heart clean of wickedness, Jerusalem, so that you may be saved. How long will the thoughts of your toils remain in you?" By "the thoughts of her toils" he means the thoughts formed in wickedness, for which she will be punished unless she washes herself with the instruction of the Scriptures. Then, since not only the soul is called to salvation but also the body itself, which the soul uses as an instrument for its own activities, it is right that the body too should be sanctified. This happens through what divine teaching calls "the washing of regeneration," which is also called divine baptism. It is no longer mere water, for it is sanctified by a mystical invocation. See how great and powerful it is by attending to the initiation that the Savior gave his disciples. He says: "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe," and so on. One must first be made a disciple by receiving the doctrines of truth. Then one must keep what he commanded them about the moral virtues, and only then be baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. If that is so, how can the water received along with all this still be mere water? It has shared, as far as possible, in the power of the Holy Trinity and is joined with both moral and intellectual virtue. Consider its greatness also by attending to why it is received. If it is received in order to enter the kingdom of God, and the kingdom surpasses everything in excellence, how can the means of entering it not be great? The kingdom of God should be understood as the state of those who live in an orderly way according to his laws. This kingdom will also have its dwelling in its own proper place, I mean in heaven. Here it is called the kingdom of God, while in Matthew it is called the kingdom of heaven. We should say that Matthew named it after those who are ruled, or after the places where they are, while John and Luke named it after God who reigns. In the same way, when we speak of the kingdom of the Romans, we identify it by those who are ruled. We indicate it either by the place [?] its land [?], or when we speak of it as the kingdom of the inhabited world.

These words point to the following meaning. The Holy Spirit comes only to the earnest, and stays far from the wicked. "Far" and "near" must not be taken in a spatial sense, but in the way such terms can be understood of incorporeal beings. Such expressions, which are often written about God too, do not mean distances in space. The Spirit, then, keeps apart from the wicked and fills those who have faith and virtue, so it is fittingly said: "The Spirit blows where it wills." This also shows that the Spirit is a substance. It is not, as some think, merely an activity of God, without a distinct existence of its own, as they hold. After listing the gifts of the Spirit, the apostle immediately added: "All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each one individually as it wills." If it wills, works and distributes, then it is an active substance and not merely an activity. And the words "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us," spoken in the Acts, are not far from willing and wishing. Besides this, the divine Scriptures record words of the Spirit, especially in the Acts of the Apostles: "While they were fasting and worshiping the Lord, the Holy Spirit said, 'Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them.'" And again in the same book a prophet named Agabus says: "Thus says the Holy Spirit: 'This is how they will bind the man who owns this belt,'" and so on. But although the Spirit blows where it wills, Nicodemus did not have it within him, because he had not believed in Jesus as he should. He heard only its voice and did not know where it goes or where it comes from. Whoever reads the writings of the Spirit without understanding them hears only its voice. But everyone who attends to the reading and searches the Scriptures with understanding knows where the Spirit's path begins and where it ends, the path it travels through the instruction of the divine oracles. Whoever knows the reason why the Spirit's teaching was given to people knows where it comes from. And whoever has also considered why it was given and for what end knows where it goes and comes to rest.

It is worth asking how the Savior could say that he had spoken of earthly things, when he had taught about the kingdom of God, birth from above and the Holy Spirit, and about being born of the Spirit. None of these is earthly; each of them is heavenly. In reply one might say that Jesus did not say, "If I told you things made of earth," but "things on earth." By "things on earth" he meant things that can exist for people still living on earth and be understood by them. They are not earthly by nature. They are heavenly, but have been given to human beings as God's gift. James writes that the things given to people are from above and heavenly: "Every good gift and every perfect present is from above, coming down from the Father of lights." He said this having learned it from the Savior, who said: "The Father will give good things from heaven to those who ask him." Of the things God supplies, some can be brought within reach of those who know in part. Others are for those who have reached perfection in the age to come, when what is partial will be done away with because the perfect has come. So it is very fittingly said: "How will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?" Whoever does not believe in the partial things will not believe in the perfect ones either.

God had commanded the serpent to be made so that the people led by Moses might know something. Because they had not believed God, who had promised them the land, they were being killed by venomous creatures. In the same way, they would be saved by gazing at the serpent that had been lifted up, because of God who had commanded it to be made. It was not the nature of the object that brought them salvation, but the one who commanded them to make it. In the same way, spiritual serpents brought human beings under death through sins, injecting them with the venom of their own wickedness. Much death had come upon souls (this is the death that follows sin). So God, being entreated, was pleased to have his own Son lifted up, so that all who look to him in faith might be freed from the harm of the spiritual serpents and have eternal life. Eternal life is not the ordinary life that other living creatures also have, but the life that grows within us from faith and the other virtues.

This passage can also be used to refute those who say that the title "Son" applies only to the one born of Mary, and not to God the Word. For see, the Son of God is the one who was sent into the [?] world. What was sent into the world was not what was taken from the Virgin (for that came into being here, born of her). It was God the Word, who is truth and the true light. Those who pray to God about him say: "Send out your light and your truth." And again it is written: "God sent out his word and healed them."

Someone will say that this interpretation, that Jesus has not now come to judge the world, is not very intelligently conceived. He will cite the words that follow: "This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world." And in this same Gospel Jesus says: "I have come into the world for judgment." This difficulty must therefore be resolved. Although by his coming Jesus does both, judging the world and saving it, one is for the sake of the other. He came into the world for judgment in order to save it (he does not save in order to judge), just as a physician comes to a sick person in order to heal him. Healing is the purpose of the physician's visit, even if other things happen too, such as cutting or cauterizing. He does not come primarily to cut [?], but to heal. Next after this comes: "Whoever believes in him is not judged." Whoever has reached complete salvation through faith is not subject to judgment. But whoever has not believed is self-condemned and has already been judged.

This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness rather than light. If the light had not come into the world, those who did not do good things could have pleaded ignorance of them. Those who practiced vices would have had grounds for a defense, claiming they had not known these things were evil. But since the light has come into the world, every misguided defense is banished. There will be a judgment that examines the deeds and the mind of each person. Those who loved the light will be accepted and receive the kingdom of God. Through their love for the light, they themselves have become light by good works and a true mind, so that they hate the darkness (that is, vice and impiety). But those who turned away from virtue, and from God who provides it, will suffer eternal punishments. Eager to keep their evil works, they hated the light, which exposes their wicked deeds by bringing them into view. "For everyone who does wicked things hates the light." He does not want to come to it at all, so that his works will not be exposed as evil. He wants to hide them so that others will not condemn him. But although such a person hates the light, the one who works the truth comes to the light, wanting the works he does to be revealed as done in God. He spoke well in saying "He who practices wicked things" and "He who does the truth," and not [?] "he who did." [?] For it is possible for someone to turn away from vice [?] and look toward the good. It is also possible for someone who professes to rejoice in the truth to lean at some point toward what is worse. That is why he said "practices" and "does." One who is given over to vice cannot rejoice in the good, and the lover of truth is certainly one who longs for good things. Coming or not coming to the light must be understood not in terms of place but in terms of action: everyone who acts according to virtue comes to it. The wicked person, who practices vice, refuses to be with the light. Good and evil cannot exist together, nor can light and darkness (here light is the same as the good, and darkness the same as evil). Those who belong to the heresies think that some people are in darkness by nature and love it. Notice, then, that the passage shows that each of them is in darkness and loves it by choice. For it says, "People loved [?] darkness rather than light," because their works were evil. It is not because they belong to darkness that their works are evil. It is because their works are evil that they love darkness. Again, it is not because they fail to come to the light that they do wicked things. It is because they do wicked things that they do not come to the light. It is in our power to do wicked things, or to [come to] the light and do the truth.

Since it is written, "People loved [?] darkness rather than light," we must ask whether they loved both, loving the darkness more and the light less. This might seem to apply to people who are neither very wicked nor perfect in virtue. But I do not think that is what is meant, namely that they love both, loving the darkness more or the light more. The meaning is rather this. Human beings have free will because they have free choice. They ought to accept the light and flee the darkness. But those whose works are evil have done the opposite: they loved the darkness and did not love the light at all. We must not take this comparatively, as though they had loved darkness more than light. They did not love the light at all; they hated it. That this reading is correct is shown by the passage itself. He says they loved darkness rather than light because, doing wicked things, they hate the light. If they hate it, then their love for darkness is not a matter of comparison. You can also apply this to what the apostle writes about wicked people, that they will be "lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God." This phrase too shows that they love pleasure alone and not God, and so are called lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God. And in the Psalms it is written about a wicked man: "You loved evil rather than goodness." He did not love both, loving evil more.

The words "All are coming to him" must be understood sensibly, as meaning [?]. So too with "A person cannot receive anything of himself unless it has been given from heaven." That is, a person cannot have any divine gift unless it has been given to him from heaven. God's gifts are given to those who have been prepared by faith and virtue to receive them. [John is saying:] "Learn, then, that although I have received from the Son of God the power to baptize with water for repentance, I fall far short of the one who gave it to me. And you are my witnesses that I am not saying this only now, but said it before, when people asked me whether I was the Christ. You were there when I said that I am the forerunner of the Christ, and not the Christ himself." No one should take offense, as if the words "A person cannot receive anything" were not rightly said.

Rational nature, of which the human soul is also a part, does not of itself give birth to any good thing, though it is able to receive good things. So, like a woman, it is made by nature to bring forth from another the virtues it can bear, both practical and intellectual. That is why I call it a bride: not the bride of any chance comer, but only of the one who sows good things. And he is none other than Jesus, who you have said is baptizing, to whom I have borne witness, and to whom, you say, everyone is coming. If, then, you too wish to bear good things, go to him. For you are part of the bride, since you belong to rational nature. But though he is the bridegroom, I am his friend, a servant of his will, and my aim is to present to him those whom I teach. So even though you have become my disciples, I am not the bridegroom, that is, I am not the perfect teacher. That is why I urge you too, now that it is [?] time for you to be joined to the perfect teacher, to go over to him, just as I myself pray to be his hearer; for I rejoice to hear his voice. And so it is our joy when those who first studied with me gain so great a capacity for understanding that they can take in the wisdom he teaches to the worthy. For you know that he who comes from above is above all, being king and almighty. And if he is above all, he is clearly above me as well; hence he must increase, and I must decrease. In this sense we should also take what Paul wrote to the Corinthians, which runs: "I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ." Here he calls the whole church the bride, a pure virgin because of the soundness of its doctrines and its way of life. And the same apostle, writing to another church, mentions Adam and his wife and then adds: "This mystery is great; but I am speaking about Christ and the church." He means that just as they became the parents of all human beings, so Christ and the church are to be the parents of all good deeds, thoughts and words. John, then, is the friend of the bridegroom we have been discussing. He stands beside him with firm assent, because his faith in him is steadfast, and standing so, he rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. Hence he goes on to say, "This joy of mine, then, is complete," since everyone is going to Jesus. For I came to bear witness to him, so that through me all might believe in him; hence he must increase, and I must decrease. But this must be considered carefully. The Savior does not increase by gaining anything, nor does John decrease by losing anything, for each remains the same. The saying is to be understood like this. The morning star rises before the sun, to accustom the eyes to face a greater light, and it has a fixed size. At first glance it looks greater than the sun; but as the sun gradually appears, the morning star decreases. It loses nothing of its own size, but it is now being compared with the sunlight that has appeared. So too John is great in the fullness of his holiness. Jesus came after him, as had been foretold, was baptized, and received John's witness. After these events had run their course and the divinity of Jesus had been revealed, the one was shown to be the servant and the other the master.

For if he comes from above and from the Father as the Almighty, he is clearly above all. But those who think in material terms bear the image of the man of dust, and they also speak from the earth. So if they ever claim to teach, the wisdom they have is the kind James writes of: earthly, unspiritual, demonic. Isaiah also writes about such people, as being from the earth and speaking out of it; whereas the Word of God, who comes from above, is above all and speaks what he has seen and heard. The prophets too, having the word that came to them from above, speak heavenly and divine things, which they saw with the mind and heard with the ears of the inner man. For each of them will say, "Thus says the Lord," and, "The word of the Lord came to me." Solomon says this more plainly: "My words have been spoken by God." That is why it is written: "In many parts and in many ways God spoke of old to the fathers through the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us" (that is, to those living at the time of his coming) "by a Son." Indeed, he spoke to people, by way of teaching, the things he had seen and heard. These words apply to his incarnate dispensation; it would be inconsistent to take them as referring to his divinity.

"And no one receives his testimony." Yet many have received his testimony, as John himself goes on to say: "Whoever has received his testimony has set his seal to this, that God is true." How, then, can it be true that "no one receives his testimony," when some do receive it? The difficulty is to be resolved like this. Jesus, who has come from above and speaks what he has heard and seen, gives a most lofty and very great testimony about the Father and about himself. No one receives this testimony in the way he himself gives it, because his hearers, who are only beginning to receive, fall far short of the greatness of the testimony. Still, even if no one is able to receive his testimony in that way, it can be received as far as those just coming to faith are able to take it in. So "whoever has received his testimony" does not contradict the statement that no one has received it, since in one sense it is not received, [?] who, having received the testimony of Jesus, set their seal with firm assent to this, that God is true. They have learned that the one sent by him speaks the words of God, since he is not from the earth and does not speak from it. For God does not give the Spirit in part.

For even if wise men who had God within them spoke the words of God, they still had the Spirit of God only in part, since God says: "I will pour out some of my Spirit on all flesh." But the Savior, sent to speak the words of God, does not give the Spirit in part. He does not receive it first and then pass it on to others. Sent from above and being above all, he gives it as its very source. We will also interpret "No one receives his testimony" in another way. Whoever searches the Scriptures finds that they bear witness about Christ. Yet none of the Jews who read the Scriptures without examining them received the testimony [about him]. Only those who can say, "We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the law, and the prophets also wrote: Jesus," receive the testimony about him, and all such do. They set their seal to this, that God is true, who promised the gospel beforehand through the prophets. Other copies have the reading: "For he does not give the Spirit by measure." This reading too indicates that the one who was sent does not deal in measures, giving sparingly, in part, and to a few who could easily be counted. Rather, he gives abundantly and richly to all who are found worthy to receive.

The heretics twist their minds in every way. They divide the Godhead, and so they assign the Old Scripture to one god and the New Testament to another. They claim that John said "He who is from the earth speaks from the earth" about himself and the other prophets, and "He whom God has sent speaks his words" about Christ and his apostles. They must be refuted, for this teaching of theirs is false, or rather impious. For the Baptist himself says about himself: "He who sent me to baptize with water said to me, 'The one on whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.' And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God." Now if the one who sent him to baptize is the Father, who told him about the descent of the Spirit, and if Christ is his Son, how can John be speaking from the earth when he says what he heard from the Father of Christ? Besides, the evangelist writes about him: "There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light." And if the prophets before John spoke from the earth, how do they bear witness about Christ? For the Savior said of their writings: "These are the ones that bear witness about me."

For how could God, who hates all wickedness, fail to love? Of him it is written: "I am God, who loves righteousness and hates robbery gained by injustice." God hates the forms of wickedness in which the sinner delights. He loves the Son, then, as the one who bestows virtue and who destroys and does away with wickedness. That is why it is said, "The Father loves the Son." He is also loved by the Son, though here again "love" is a word heard in human terms, not understood in them. For when God loves righteousness, he does not love it as a righteous man does, so as to possess it within himself and be shaped by it. It is in such a way that he longs for the Son, who is Word, truth, wisdom and sanctification. The phrase may also be meant to show the close kinship of the Father with the Son. For it is a law of nature that parents love their offspring. Among human beings, affection for one's children comes by nature, while affection for things loved in other ways arises differently. In the same way God loves the world as God, but loves the Son as Father. That is why it does not say "The [?]," but "The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand." This must be understood faithfully and wisely. If "all things came into being through him," then all things are under his hand by reason of creation and providence. But through sin they departed and went outside the hand that sheltered them. So for their salvation the Father gives them into the hand of the Son. In doing so he grants no addition to the Son, but improvement to them. He gives them to him as to a teacher and a physician, so that, having freed them from ignorance and disease, that is, from wickedness, he may keep them sheltered and ruled by him, now that he holds them under his active and provident hand. The truth of this interpretation is shown by what follows: "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life." For if whoever believes in the Son has eternal life once he has been given into the Son's hand, then he is given for his own salvation and improvement, and not so that the Son may have something more. And when is the giving of all things into the Son's hand fulfilled, if not when every knee shall bow to him, in heaven and on earth and under the earth?

In many places in Scripture, the punishments inflicted on the wicked are called the wrath of God. For example, Moses says of the Egyptians: "You sent out your wrath, and it consumed them like stubble." And Paul writes of the Jews: "But wrath has come upon them to the uttermost," calling "wrath" the punishments that God brought upon them. And to the one who despises God's kindness and patience he says: "Because of your hardness and your impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath." We must not suppose that what is called God's wrath is a passion in God. How could a passion belong to the one who is beyond passion? Since God is unchangeable and does not undergo passion, what is called his wrath must be interpreted in the way just described.

He truly had a body, made up of the same things as every human body. So his body too was necessarily subject to the common passions. I mean not only wounds and the like, but also the weariness that comes from very strenuous and continuous movement. At midday, when the sun is scorching, he had completed a long journey and grown very weary, the moisture of his body drained by the blazing heat; for it was the sixth hour of the day. Wanting to rest from this weariness, he sat down at the spring in the field of Joseph mentioned earlier. At the same time he was providing for the good of the woman who was about to come to draw water from the spring.

Someone may perhaps ask why Jews have no dealings with Samaritans. The reason can be found in 1 and 2 Kings, and also in 2 Chronicles. Because the law had said, "Do not touch anything unclean," they did not dare to touch even the flesh of foreigners, believing it would defile them. Someone may also object to the words "His disciples had gone away into the city to buy food." He may say: "In the wilderness he fed five thousand and four thousand, besides a crowd of women and a great number of children, once from five loaves and once from seven. What great thing would it have been to supply his disciples with food without their going into the city to buy it, if Jesus had provided it by his own power?" To this we must reply as follows. Jesus had become man. If he had done everything purely as God, no one would have known that he had become man, just as, if he had done everything as [?], his divinity would have been hidden. So whenever there was need for a miracle, he fed many from a little, not so much to satisfy their hunger as to reveal his divine power. But when there was no pressing need to provide plenty of food where there was none, the disciples went off to buy bread. Jesus did these things to show his humanity and reveal his divinity, and even so many stumbled at the gospel. Some declared that he became man only in appearance and not in truth; others took him to be a mere man. How much more, then, would careless and unthinking readers of the account have been led astray if nothing had been done and written with care to reveal both his divinity and his humanity?

The Samaritan woman did her utmost to exalt Samaritan belief and set it above Jewish customs and doctrines. That is why, when the Savior promised to give her living water, she retorted, "Are you greater than our father Jacob?" But the Savior knew how to arrange everything wisely. He knew that to exalt the things of the Jews and to say "Greater" would immediately offend the mind of a woman who as yet imagined nothing higher than what the senses perceive. So he stored that answer away in silence. Instead he used other words, no less able to make the point but gentler to the ear, and so made her more ready to receive it. He does not make the comparison or speak of the difference in glory himself; he leaves the woman to work out the vastness of his superiority from what he goes on to say. "Whoever drinks of this water," he says, "will thirst again; but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst again." Notice the wisdom and the power of these words. He said "will thirst again" as something needing no proof from elsewhere, for the woman herself was a ready witness to it. But with "will never thirst again" [?] he drew her in, stirring her by the greatness of the promise. Through both statements he leads her toward a more divine understanding, as if saying: "If you hold Jacob in higher honor and count it a marvelous achievement that he gave you water, though whoever drinks it returns to the same thirst, what should you think of one who can give water that does more than ease bodily thirst for a short time? This water can become in the one who drinks it a spring of ever-flowing water, providing streams of salvation that water those who draw from them and bring them life [?]." For just as water cures thirst and cleans the dirt from the outside of the body, so the spiritual and heavenly streams of Jesus' teaching, and a more divine understanding of him, heal the thirst that comes from unbelief. They also cleanse the soul of the filth with which the defilement of sins and the dark reasoning of impious opinions had soiled it.

Taken allegorically, the well of Jacob must be said to be the scripture of Moses. Jacob and his sons drank from it spiritually, and Jacob's livestock drank from it too. By "livestock" we are to understand allegorically those who are steady and gentle but lack reason. These may properly be called the herds and flocks of Jacob.

If, then, the law given through Moses is the water, how could Jesus say that whoever drinks of it will thirst again? We must answer that the law was given to people not so that they would live by it forever, but only until a certain time. So drinking from the well we have been interpreting was meant to last until a greater water was revealed. For the commandments of the law were laid down only until the time of reformation. That is why whoever drinks the water of the law will thirst again, longing for the drink of the gospel. This is how you should take what is said in Isaiah: "Drink this first; act quickly." If there were nothing else to drink afterward, it would not have said, "Drink this first." Since the gospel succeeds the law, whoever drinks the teaching of the law will thirst again, so as to drink the teaching of the gospel as well. But the gospel has no successor, so whoever drinks from it will never thirst again. For Jesus said, "Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away." He says that whoever drinks this water gains within himself a spring, not of ordinary water, but of water welling up to eternal life. This water, welling up to life, lifts up the one who has it and raises him to life, since it is a spring within him.

When the woman said she wanted to receive water from Jesus to quench her thirst, she showed that she wanted it so as to have it as a spring within herself. With these words she admitted that drawing the former water was hard labor, and in this she spoke the truth, for keeping the law according to the letter is hard labor indeed. The Savior fittingly replies to her, in effect: "Since the law, to which you gave yourself and with which you live as with a husband, still holds you, go and call it. Then you can compare what is written in it with what I say and do. In this way you will be able to discover that whoever drinks of the former water will look for another, because he will thirst again." When she denied having a husband, the Savior gently exposed her Samaritan way of thinking and said: "You are right to say that you have no husband." That is, you have not given your full assent to the whole Old Testament, which is the law, of which it is written: "Christ is the end of the law, for righteousness." Not having this husband, you have had five, because you assented only to what is perceptible to the senses in Scripture. If you had lived with the whole of the Old Testament, you would have been able to recognize God the Word, who was awaited after the law and the prophets. "For you have had five husbands" is to be referred to the five books of Moses, since the Samaritans accept these alone. And who is the sixth, the one she has besides the five husbands, who is not even her husband? We must say that he is the statement that Jesus is a prophet. She had already assented to this, but because she was compelled by what had been said, not with true assent. So it is fittingly said, "And the one you have now is not your husband," for you have not truly given yourself to him. Her five husbands were said to be the things perceptible to the senses. After them she assented, without real understanding, to a spiritual word from Jesus' teaching. So it is said most aptly: "And the spiritual word you now seem to have is not your husband."

When you hear that salvation is from the Jews, understand the words as referring to the one who speaks them. For he himself was the expectation of the nations, born of the seed of David according to the flesh.

"Has anyone brought him something to eat?" shows that he accepted the services of those who brought him things, even though he was able to feed others rather than be fed. To feed Christ is a deed of the very highest worth, and he did not begrudge it to those who wished to do it; that is why he gave the disciples the same task. Being learned in the law and lovers of study, and seeing that it was now mealtime, they guessed that food had been brought to Jesus. They remembered how at God's command Habakkuk carried a meal to Daniel in Babylon, and how Elijah on his journey was given food by an angel and by ravens. Yet even if the disciples were thinking of physical food, he himself makes clear what kind of food he had spoken to them about. I said it was mealtime for him for the following reasons. It was the sixth hour of the day when Jesus sat down at the spring and talked with the Samaritan woman, while the disciples had gone to buy food. So by now one might reckon that it was evening. And evening is the time for a meal, especially for those whose first concern is not food but the good of those who come to them.

He calls Judea his homeland, and this is also why he left it. For the evangelist, explaining why he went to Galilee, writes: "A prophet has no honor in his own homeland." This testimony is also found in the other Gospels, where the Savior says: "A prophet is not without honor except in his own homeland, among his relatives, and in his own house." Indeed, all the prophets before his coming were dishonored in Jerusalem and Judea, for this was their land and their homeland. So the Savior could say of them all: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you!"

“Now there is,” it says, “in Jerusalem,” and so on. He judged it unnecessary to go about healing every sick person, whoever they might be, so that he would not earn a reputation for self-display. Instead he healed one, and through that one made himself known to all. For this reason he went to the Sheep Pool, which had five porticoes: besides the four around it, it had another in the middle. It was called the Sheep Pool because the sheep brought for the feasts were gathered there, and because, when the sheep were sacrificed, their entrails were washed in that water. This is why a great crowd of people suffering from various illnesses had gathered in the place in hope of healing, as though the water must surely have some power, since the entrails of what was brought to God and sacrificed were thrown into it. God, working along with this belief of theirs, caused a stirring of the water to happen at certain unknown times. Believing that this was brought about by some divine power, they went down and received healing. Many were not healed at the same time, but only the first to go down enjoyed the grace, so that the ease of healing would not lessen the wonder. And by keeping more watchful and waiting for the stirring of the water with great earnestness, they were taught to keep the proper frame of mind even after their healing. So although there were many sick people, he did not heal them all. To show his own power, he chose one, the one held by the most serious affliction, who because of the length of time had no hope of recovery. For there was among them a paralytic who had been held by the affliction for thirty-eight years. He went to this man and did not at once say, “Take up your mat and walk,” but began his conversation with him from a natural sequence of words, just as he had also done with the Samaritan woman.

Inc.: "But what Spirit was not yet?" Expl.: "...was seen in none of the prophets; they worked wonders."

I think this was said to show that the spittle of Christ had a healing power. And although the blind man did not himself ask to receive his sight, he will still be found praiseworthy for offering himself to Jesus as he anointed his eyes with clay, and for doing what he was commanded without hesitation, even though Jesus had not told him that he would see. But perhaps the Lord's spittle was a symbol of a word [?] that is, as it were, the highest among words, a greater than which human nature cannot contain. But since such a word does not come to human beings stripped of matter and bodily illustrations, Jesus therefore spits on the ground and makes clay. See, then, whether, in giving an account of the whole of Scripture and the manner of its narration, you can say that it is made up of the spittle of Christ because of its divine meanings, and of the earth on the ground because of its narration, which takes the form of histories and human affairs. Thus the whole letter of the law and the prophets and the other scriptures would come from clay of this kind, with which one must anoint the eyes of those who do not see; and after this one must go away to Siloam, that is, to the One Sent by God. By this is signified a kind of swimming, as it were, in inquiries and in perplexities about the truth; for Job says somewhere, "But a mortal swims about idly in words." Let us therefore wash off, in the water of the pool of "the One Sent," the clay smeared on our eyes, so that after this we may be able to see. You will understand the clay to be the first elements of the oracles of God, by which we are fed with milk like infants; but when the things of the infant are done away with and we partake of solid food, we cast off the clay, so that we may return to Jesus seeing. All these things turn on the Son of God, for in his various aspects he is himself also the One Sent. Take the human things as coming before Siloam, but refer the water that is sent, and Siloam, to his more divine things. And in Isaiah too you will understand that the divine and steadfast word is signified by these things, while Rezin and the son of Remaliah stand for the words of the Gentiles and of those who hold other opinions. For how else did the people want kings in place of the water of Siloam, and how is the king of the Assyrians and all his power the water of a river, strong and abundant, unless he too is some opposing power that floods with the mass of its persuasive arguments the Judea that does not want the water of Siloam, and prevails over it? That he did not heal the man on the spot, but commanded him to go away and wash, and granted him healing once he had washed, was a deliberate arrangement so that the miracle that took place would escape no one's notice. For just as he commanded the paralytic to take up his bed on a day on which it was not lawful to do so, so that everyone who accused him of breaking the law might thereby learn the greatness of the miracle that had occurred, so too he commanded this man, who was far from the pool, to go away and wash.

The beggar begs because he lacks the necessities and is unable to provide for himself in a more respectable way. You might find such people among the Greeks and barbarians who profess the truth, begging for help, as it were, for lack of a fitting provision [?] from the speculations of the truth that are rich in reason [?] without hindrance. But the word forbids such inquiry when it says somewhere: "Child, do not live a beggar's life; it is better to die than to beg." The unjust steward in the Gospels is ashamed to beg, and for this reason he said to the one who owed a hundred measures of wheat, "Take your bill and write sixty," and to the one who owed a hundred measures of oil, "Take your bill and make it eighty." He preferred taking from the one who owed his master to begging in shame, and for this he was praised. So Jesus freed the man blind from birth not only from his blindness but also from begging. For together with sight he gave him the understanding of how he would provide himself with what is necessary for the salvation of the soul. Here, then, blindness is the cause of begging, but in the Acts it is lameness; and the man freed from these will beg no longer.

If, as the Pharisees supposed, the one who does not keep what they considered the sabbath is not from God, yet the priests in the temple who profane the sabbath were from God, then it was not evident that one who does not keep their sabbath is not from God. So the statement was not made by all the Pharisees of that time; rather, "some of the Pharisees" said it, as the evangelist says. Notice too that the words "such signs" are not set down idly. For there are different kinds of signs, so that, as the apostle says, both the one under the law and the lawless one, whom the Lord will destroy with the breath of his mouth, work them, with all power and lying signs and wonders, and God works them through the prophets; "such" is said because the signs done through Christ surpass the others in being both true and great on earth. But if anyone, supposing that the saying "How can a man who is a sinner do such signs?" is not sound, *** on reading the deeds of Samson he will say that what Samson did, such as his dealings with women, was not sin but a revealed dispensation; for the words "he did evil in the sight of the Lord" are not added.

We must observe that the evangelist, speaking in his own person, says both that the blind man's eyes were opened and that he saw: that they were opened, in the words "Now it was the sabbath on the day when he made the clay and opened his eyes"; and that he saw, in the words "And he washed and came back seeing." We will set out the difference between these expressions from Tobit: since white films had formed in his eyes, Scripture does not record that his eyes were opened, but that he saw. Throughout the whole passage about the blind man you will notice both expressions, some saying one thing and others another, and a division arising. You will also notice in Isaiah, prophesying about the coming of Christ, that he comes to open the eyes of the blind. Next one can see how the man who answers replies to the first questioners and how to the second: to the first more precisely, since they were neighbors and had seen him before when he was a beggar; but to the Pharisees he told nothing about Siloam, nor that the Savior made the clay, nor that he commanded him anything. Perhaps the man who was healed saw that the questioning of the first group had [?], while that of the second had malice, and so answered each accordingly.

Besides lying, they also sinned in another way, by exposing their own son to obvious harm. I think there is also a reason for this: in opening the eyes of the blind man, Christ opened the eyes not of a child but of one who was of age, so that he might see as a man. The other blind men who received their sight were of this kind too. And it is true that one who is of age can speak for himself, especially when Jesus has made him see. For such a man has no need of someone else to plead on his behalf.

Here "You did not listen" is equivalent to "You did not accept, you did not want [?]." And "Why then do you want to hear it again?" amounts to: "Why, you people, do you now want to hear? For you want to hear in vain if you do not believe me when I tell the truth." With this he invites everyone who learns what happened to him to become a disciple of the one who taught something more divine than all human teaching.
The words "Here is a marvel" carry a noteworthy implication. For it is a marvel if where Jesus comes from is known by ordinary people; for they do not see his root and source, the Father.

If so great a doctrine were true, that a sinner is not heard by God, it would not have been passed over in silence, but would have been stated by someone worthy of belief, for example by the servant of God or by one of the prophets. And if God did not hear a sinner, how were sinners taught to say, "Forgive us our trespasses, as we also forgive our debtors"? Whom, then, does God hear? Those who are inclining toward repentance, even if they have not yet ceased to be sinners. If God did not hear sinners, our Savior would not have eaten and drunk with tax collectors and sinners. And if those who needed physicians because they were ill had not been heard, he would not have healed them. Therefore, since the prayer of those who have sinned but are not wholly unbelieving accomplishes something, it is said, "If you, Lord, should mark iniquities, Lord, who will stand?" But perhaps he is speaking not of just anything in a sinner's prayer, but of works as great as were the works of Jesus. For when sinners ask God for works of that kind, he does not hear them.

Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and having found him he said to him, "Do you believe in the Son of Man?" Because the Jews had cast him out from among them on account of his boldness in speaking for the Savior, for this reason Jesus found him. If the Savior came to seek and to save what was lost, and the goal of one who seeks is to find what he is seeking, it is clear that the words "having found him" must not be taken simply. For it was then above all that he had to be found, when he was cast out by those who did not accept the testimony about Jesus. Once he was outside their company he became fit to be found. The words "Jesus heard that they had cast him out" must also be understood more intelligently. For having heard of such a thing, he finds the man he had heard about, who was worthy of his hearing. And having found him, he asked the one who had been found, "Do you believe in the Son of Man who has found you?" And perhaps the one who is beginning believes in the Son of Man, while the one who is advancing goes up also to believing in the Son of God, so that he might say: "Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him according to the flesh only, but also as Son of God." But how does the one who knows all things ask questions? See whether you will answer this by citing "The Lord knew those who are his" and "I do not know you." For a person is not worthy to be known as soon as he is found, as in the words "But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by him." Rather, after the introduction there must be progress, so that one may be seen and known by God. This is why the Savior questions him, saying, "Do you believe in the Son of Man?" But since he could not yet say, "I believe," but answered as one who did not know, "Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?", he was, so to speak, on the border between unbelief and faith. This is why the Savior says to him, "You have seen him, and the one speaking with you is he."

For such a tradition and opinion prevailed among the Jews; hence the disciples too asked Jesus, "Did this man sin, or his parents?" But the Lord declared, "Neither this man nor his parents," as was discussed earlier.

We must not pass lightly over the fact that "you have seen" refers to past time and "the one speaking with you" to the present, meaning that the one who was seen is the same as the one now speaking with him. Compare: "Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." For many who had seen him did not know him. So the one who has truly seen him is the one whose soul's eyes are enlightened by God himself. The man who was once blind, then, benefited from both, from seeing and from the word, and not only said, "I believe, Lord," but also worshiped him.
LXXIII a.
From Eustathius, On the Witch of Endor 21 [p. 60, ed. Jahn].

No less, when he (that is, Origen) examines the episode of the stoning, since he tries to allegorize this too, he misrepresents the letter of the Gospel, saying: "We did not find at all, when we searched in what comes before, that the Jews picked up stones to stone him." Then a little later he says: "For if they picked them up again, they had picked them up before."

If they picked them up again, they had picked them up before. Since, then, we do not overlook that this is written, we must look for the reason why "again" was added. I think that whoever speaks evil throws a kind of stone at the one he slanders. They had spoken evil of him earlier, when "a division arose among the Jews because of his words." So again, taking up the weight of slanderous words as though they were stones to be hurled at him, they rushed to stone him with their abuse. This is why Wisdom says, "Whoever throws a stone on high throws it on his own head." For one who speaks unrighteousness on high is said to throw a stone on high. You will find in divine Scripture a mixture of what is, as it were, historical with what serves to exercise the mind, especially in John. Notice in the conversation with the Samaritan woman how "Jesus sat by the well" is a narrative about a physical well and a perceptible body; but it is no longer possible to understand it of physical drink when "Jesus answered and said to her, 'If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, "Give me a drink," you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.'" So too here: "I have shown you many good works; for which of these works are you stoning me?" If anyone goes back and gathers from the beginning of the Gospel the works of Jesus, referring them to spiritual activities, he above all will see what many works he showed to those who picked up stones to stone Jesus. For example, one of his good works was the sign at Cana, when the earlier wine ran out because "the law and the prophets were until John," [?] and we, with whom Jesus reclines at table, have an abundance of the good wine. And this is indeed the beginning of his signs in the calling of the people from the Gentiles; for it is also written, "This beginning of signs Jesus did." Next after this is his restoring the house of his [?], which had become a house of trade, so that it became once again the house of his Father. And why need I list all the good works he has done from his Father?

So that he might not make his divinity too plainly manifest by staying longer among those eager to seize him without being seized, and so debase the pattern of the human order. Consider whether there may be some reason why it is not written simply, "He went away to the [?]," but beyond and "across" it. Just as those who received their inheritance of the land through Moses, being inferior to those who received theirs through Joshua, were allotted their inheritance across the Jordan; there they built an altar as a symbol of the altar in the holy land, but they did not offer sacrifice or whole burnt offerings on it. But by now we understand more figuratively the words "He went away across the Jordan to the place where John was baptizing at first." And indeed Joshua the son of Nun leads the people over from across the Jordan with wondrous mighty works. And Elijah too, when he was about to be taken up as if into heaven in a chariot of fire and with horses of fire, crossed from the far side of the Jordan, having parted the stream of the river with his mantle.

They sought again to seize him, and he escaped from their hand. In the anagogical sense, there are some who want to hunt down the Christian teaching in order to overturn and destroy it; these may now be said to be seeking to seize Jesus. But since "Wisdom will not enter a soul that devises evil" and "Power, when put to the test, exposes the foolish," therefore he escapes; when the word of truth seems to those who hold it to be in their hand, it gets out of their hand, and they cannot hold it fast. That is why even when they seem to overturn it, they do not overturn the truth, for they themselves do not understand. And having escaped from their hand, he comes to the river Jordan, which is interpreted [?], where the heavens are opened and bear witness to the Word: "This is the Son of God, in whom the Father is well pleased." And even if someone happens to be across the river, yet if he draws near to it he will find Jesus baptizing with a better baptism than John's. For John first baptized with the perceptible baptism, but Jesus with the spiritual, since he baptized with the Holy Spirit and with fire, rather like the fire seen on the bush that did not consume it. Pay careful attention to the words "where John was baptizing at first," which are ambiguous, and having seen both meanings of the expression, decide which of them you should accept. Either John first baptized across the Jordan and afterwards in Aenon near Salim, so that Jesus went away across the Jordan to the place where John had baptized before the baptism he performed at Aenon; or else this: John baptized with the first baptism across the Jordan, and Jesus the Christ baptized with the second baptism where John had baptized when he gave the first baptism. The second seems to me more reasonable than the first. But one might say something like this about the first interpretation too: John gives the first baptism across the Jordan, which is interpreted [?], and the second in Aenon near Salim. Aenon is interpreted "Eye of [?]," and Salim "He himself the [?]." Those who receive the second washing, then, are already more clear-sighted, having acquired the eye of the soul through much trial and toil. And it was fitting that the first baptism should be at a descent and the second with one who is ascending.

We find the name of Lazarus twice in the Gospels: first in Luke, in the parable of the rich man and the man called Lazarus, when he died and went away to Abraham's bosom; second in the passage before us. Is it a case of the same name borne by two Lazaruses, or is that one this one? For anyone who wants to say that both evangelists are speaking of one man will claim that during the three days in between (for Lazarus rose on the fourth day) he was carried away by the angels to Abraham's bosom and rested there; and that because of what the rich man said in the words "I beg you, then, father, to send him to my father's house, so that they too may not come to this place of torment," he was not sent by Abraham, who said, "They have Moses and the prophets"; but our Savior and Lord raised him, perhaps so that he might report, though this is passed over in silence, what he had seen and how the affairs of souls are ordered. But this is nonsense. For the Lazarus in the story of the rich man was destitute and cast out at the gate, whereas this one had Mary and Martha as sisters, who were well-to-do and well known among the Jews, so that they even received Jesus as a guest. And hear what the evangelist John himself says: "It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment." Would the woman who had ointment and was loved by Jesus not have taken pity on her brother as he longed to be fed with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table? That would make no sense. He was from Bethany, which is interpreted "House of [?]." Perhaps everyone from Bethany who has made obedience his own is a friend of Jesus. But since human nature is changeable, even a friend of Jesus may sometimes fall ill; and he would fall ill if Jesus were not present with him, and not only fall ill but also die.

It is clear that Mary is the same woman who in Luke too anointed the Lord with ointment. But he passed over her name in silence, while John supplied what Luke had left out. And who would not be moved by such testimony from Jesus about Mary not to despair of himself because of his former deeds, but to come and sit at Jesus' feet and become his disciple? For she too, it says, "was a woman in the city, a sinner," who, "having learned that he was reclining at table in the Pharisee's house, brought an alabaster jar of ointment, and standing behind him at his feet, weeping, began to wet his feet with her tears." One might say that Mary is a symbol of those from the Gentiles, Martha of those from the circumcision, and their brother who rises from the dead a symbol of those who have gone down to Hades because of certain sins, according to the words "Let sinners be turned back to Hades." And not implausibly he will say that it was because of the way of life under the law of Moses that Martha was told, "Martha, Martha, you are troubled and distracted about many things, but few things are needed." For salvation does not require the many commandments according to the letter of the law, but a few, on which hang the whole law and the prophets: those that legislate love.

Taken as a symbol, let it signify death in the historical sense; but with respect to the anagogical sense, let it present the death into which those whose soul's eyes have not been enlightened by God sometimes fall asleep. Yet not all who are unenlightened fall asleep into death; it is only among the things that may happen *** And this is why the psalmist says, "Enlighten my eyes, lest I sleep in death"; and pay careful attention to the word "lest." So he told the disciples plainly, since at first he had spoken in figures, "Lazarus has fallen asleep," and "I am glad for your sake that I was not there." For if he had been there, Lazarus would not have died, since it is impossible for anyone to die when Jesus is present. But for the dead man to rise from the dead, Jesus must come to the one who has died.

"For your sake," he says, "I am glad" that you come to believe by learning that he died while I was not with him, and so that you may be confirmed in the faith. He alone, then, wakes Lazarus. But it was the disciples' task to loose him, a dead man bound hand and foot with grave-bands, his face wrapped in a cloth, held by the bonds of the dead, and to let him go, as Jesus commanded. Thomas says, "Let us go, so that we may die with him." Thomas had read the prophecies about the Savior. It is also likely that he had heard that a work still remained for the Son of God concerning souls, which he was to carry out by going down to their place, so as to go and preach to the spirits in prison, who had once been disobedient. Hearing "I am going to wake him," he thought that Lazarus would be woken and raised from the dead only if Jesus went down into the place of souls. The Savior had also said, "No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of myself," and similar things. So, as his true disciple, having resolved to follow him wherever he might go, Thomas wished that he and the rest of the disciples might, by the grace of Jesus, lay down the body together with him. Perhaps he also understood that it would not be possible to live with Jesus without dying with him, as Paul also holds. But those who do not want him to have spoken for this reason will say that he said it because he foresaw the envy the Jews would feel at Lazarus's rising, and the danger that would follow. "When Jesus came, then, he found that he had been there four days." The number four is material and bodily, and so it is a number of affliction, since the elemental bodies are four. Hence those who are enslaved and afflicted suffer for four hundred years, as it is said: "They will afflict them and humble them for four hundred years." Perhaps it is for this reason, for the cleansing of the sins that follow from the nature of the body, that Moses fasts forty days, and Elijah likewise, and the Savior for our sins. And now, then, Jesus came and found Lazarus already four days in the tomb, which is the dwelling of the dead. For to sinners tombs are houses, which is why the demon-possessed also flee to the tombs as to a place of their own. As long as they are inside, no one is able to pass along that road. But when they come out, they put off their nakedness, are decently clothed, are in their right mind, and sit at the feet of Jesus. Jesus, however, is laid in a new tomb and wrapped in a clean linen cloth, and he does not reach the fourth day among the dead. That is why he was "free among the dead," and he is raised on the free and holy number three. By this number he also sanctifies us with the washing of water, saying that we must be baptized into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Spirit.
