Bethany is interpreted "House of obedience"; Jerusalem [?]. It is near, then, at a distance of fifteen stadia, the same as the number of the temple steps. The number fifteen divides into the seven of the Sabbath and the eight of circumcision, the only numbers to which Ecclesiastes urges us to give a portion: "Give a portion," he says, "to seven and also to eight." Suppose Mary is a symbol of the contemplative life, Martha of the active life, and Lazarus of one who has fallen into sins after coming to faith. Then it is fitting that Mary and Martha mourn Lazarus, and in their mourning they need consolation for their brother. The Jews want to offer them this consolation [?] words before the fullness of time [?], but they despair of being able to stop the dead man's sister from [grieving] over the dead. Martha now seems more eager than Mary, since Martha ran to Jesus while Mary stayed sitting at home. But some, like the centurion, are not fit to receive Jesus, while others are worthy, like the ruler of the synagogue. So Martha, as the lesser, ran to Jesus, while Mary waits at home to receive him, as one able to hold his visit. She would not have left her house if she had not heard her sister say, "The Teacher is here and is calling you." And when she got up, she did not simply get up, but got up quickly. And falling at Jesus' feet she said what she said, whereas the other had not fallen down before him.

The Savior is not unaware whether Martha believes what is said or not when he asks, "Do you believe this?" He asks so that we, or those present at the time, may learn her disposition from her answer. Someone else will say that he is not asking at all, but declaring: "You believe this." Then Martha, completing the Savior's declaration, says, "Yes, Lord," as if to say: I believe not only what you are saying; that you are the Christ I do not only believe now, but have believed already. And I believe that you are the Son of God who is coming into the world, and who shine forth on all who believe in you.

Someone examining the higher meaning might ask why she says, "If you had been here." Is there any place where Jesus is not? Where two or three are gathered in his name, he is there among them; and he also stands among others who do not know him. In this second way he was present to Mary and Martha, for they had not advanced far enough to recognize that he was present.

As for "Where have you laid him?", do not be surprised that it is spoken as if by someone who does not know. For in a certain sense Scripture says that not only the Savior but also the Father "does not know," as in: "If anyone among you is spiritual, let him acknowledge that what I write to you is from God; but if anyone does not acknowledge it, he is not acknowledged." He asks, "Where have you laid him?", just as he commands the disciples to leave the dead. And Jesus weeps whenever one of his friends comes to be in a tomb.

While he was still far from the tomb, he was deeply moved in spirit. But when he comes near the dead man, he is no longer moved in spirit; instead he holds the emotion in within himself. That is why it says, "Deeply moved within himself, he comes to the tomb." Again he rebukes the emotion, so that we may learn that he became a human being as we are, without undergoing change. "It was a cave, and a stone lay against it." For he had been laid not in a built tomb but in one cut out of the rock. Perhaps this is why there is woe for those who build tombs or monuments, since one ought to build houses, a temple, and whatever is useful to the living. Then he says, "Take away the stone." Since the cave was a tomb, he did not touch the stone himself but had others who were suited to the work remove it. But in Genesis a stone lay on the mouth of the well and kept the sheep from drinking, the sheep from which the marked ones and Jacob's portion were to come. That stone Jacob himself had to take hold of; he had to go up to it and roll it away. It was fitting that at the well Jacob himself should go up, but that Jesus should stand outside the cave.

It is not that whoever prophesies is a prophet; rather, whoever is a prophet prophesies. Balaam, for example, prophesies though he is a soothsayer. For if someone has done something medical, that does not yet make him a physician, nor does doing some building make him a builder. Some hold that Caiaphas did not speak from the Holy Spirit. They point out that David, after he had sinned, says, "Do not take your Holy Spirit from me," and argue that the Spirit does not dwell in a body that is in debt to sin. Instead, they say, Caiaphas spoke through the working of evil spirits. For they say that demons are sometimes able to foretell things, like the spirit of divination in Paul's case, and in the Savior's case: "Ah, what have we to do with you, Son of God?" We learn, in fact, that people do not say everything of themselves; some things they say under the working of a power, either a higher one or a worse one. But just as some heretics misconstrue [?] the sense of Scripture, so the Pharisees take what Caiaphas said in their own sense.

The Word also wishes to turn us away from rushing into dangers too rashly and too hotly, even when they are for the sake of the truth. When we are seized, we should stand firm; but when danger is still coming, we should withdraw, because the outcome is uncertain. In the higher sense it should be said that Jesus once walked openly among the Jews through the prophets, but now no longer. For the word of God is not among them. It has gone away from them into the wilderness, of which it is said, "Many more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband." It went near Ephraim, which is interpreted [?]. Ephraim is the brother of Manasseh, the elder, whose name means "from forgetfulness"; for after the people "from forgetfulness" comes the "fruitfulness" of the Gentiles. "And there he stayed with the disciples": he is present in the "fruitfulness." And at the birth of Ephraim, our Lord himself, the one who distributes our grain, who humbled himself and became obedient to death, might say, "God has made me increase in the land of my humiliation."

Whoever follows him serves him by following him, and whoever serves him is his servant; and therefore, where the Word is, there he is too. The promise is not to be understood in a bodily and local sense. But suppose that, as among bodily places, there is a region of the ether among the purest places, more translucent through the fineness of its light. Then one would not be wrong to say that those in the body who excel will receive at the resurrection, according to their worth, a body of surpassing and distinguished glory. One could say that they come to be in those regions because these are best suited to leisure for contemplating God the Word. Conceptually, it is one thing for his servant to be where God the Word is and another to be honored by the Father, but in reality they are the same. For through the honor that comes from the Father, whoever is honored comes to be where God the Word is.

At the time of the saving passion, all the powers of Satan, together with their leader [?], made war on the Savior. Seeing them, the Savior's soul was troubled in a human way. It did not fear death, though that too is human; it feared being defeated. For Christ at times allowed his soul to suffer what is proper to it. And since he was to become the cause of eternal salvation for those who obey him, his soul was grieved and troubled over them. Yet it was not, as one might think, overpowered by the trouble; the trouble lasted only an instant. This is what "now" signifies: it ceased the moment it began and was, so to speak, a mere point of time. Consider whether he himself also prays that the contest against the evil powers arrayed against him may take place not over a stretch of time but in the "now." That instant was enough for the soul of Jesus to conquer all the power of the evil one.

His suffering on the cross was the judgment of this whole world. For "having made peace through the blood of his cross, whether for things on earth or things in heaven," he triumphed on the tree over the principalities and powers he had stripped off, and sat down in the heavenly places, restoring all things to the end that suits and befits each. Since, then, it was the work accomplished on the cross that held together the judgment of every being, he said, when the time of his passion drew near, "Now is the judgment of this world."

Our Savior's passion took place for the cleansing of the foreknown, by whom the world was to be judged. For this reason it is said, "Now is the judgment of this world," as if he were saying: it is the time for revealing those who will judge the world. Or else, since the tyrant was to be overthrown at the time of the saving passion, it is said, "Now the ruler of this world will be cast out," perhaps into the outer darkness.

They convict themselves of ignorance about the prophets and show that their knowledge of the Scriptures is not exact. They had drawn from such sayings the idea that the Christ remains forever. But the mystery of the death that would come in between, and the brief separation of the soul from the body, they neither understood nor examined closely. They should have known the reason. Two comings of Christ were prophesied. The crowd of the Jews hoped for the more glorious one, which will take place at the consummation of the age, but had hardly any understanding of the one before it. Therefore their house is left to them.

To everyone who has, more will be given, and he will have abundance; in the same way, from him who has not, even what he seems to have will be taken away. So if anyone who has received the mina ties it up in a cloth, he will hear, "The light is among you for a little while longer." For "Take the mina from him" has not yet been said, since "whoever is dishonest in little is dishonest also in much." One might also explain the passage this way. Just as the kingdom of God was among the Jews, so the light too was among them. Because they did not render the fruits due to the kingdom of God, they heard, "The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation that produces its fruits." In the same way, while the light was among them, they did not walk so that darkness would not overtake them. Therefore, after the little while, the light among them was taken from them. It was given to the nation that produces the fruits of the light, which has become like the stars of heaven and is called the light of the world, having received this from him who said, "I am the light of the world."

Divine Scripture recognizes that we have free will: it blames sinners as blameworthy by their own doing, and praises those who keep the divine commandment as praiseworthy through their own agency. To see this, hear what it says in Deuteronomy: "And now, Israel, what does the Lord your God ask of you but to fear the Lord your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him and to serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, and to keep the commandments of the Lord and his ordinances, which I command you today, so that it may go well with you?" And in Micah: "Has it been told you, O man, what is good? Or what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord your God?" As far as these passages are concerned, then, each of us is able to become righteous or unrighteous. You will understand "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts" as referring to the evil one, as was said before. It is he who blinded the eyes of some and hardened their heart, so that they might not see with their eyes or understand with their heart, and turn, and the Lord heal them. For "lest they turn and he heal them" is not written with the same subject as "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart." So the one who blinds the eyes and hardens the heart is one, and the one who heals those who turn, the brokenhearted and the blind, is another. The apostle too says this in Second Corinthians: "And if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those in whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, so that the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, may not shine on them." And it is no wonder that those who submit themselves to the evil one through their sins are blinded by him in their eyes and hardened in their heart according to his will. For he does everything so that they may not see with their eyes, understand with their heart, and turn. As for "For this reason they could not believe," the answer is as follows. Take the man blind from birth, whom our Savior later healed. If someone had said, "He cannot see because he is blind," he would not have meant that the man could never see. It was possible for those who until then could not see to see afterward, since Jesus, by opening the eyes of the blind, gave sight to the blind. In the same way, some at one time could not believe because the evil one had blinded their eyes. Yet it was not impossible for them to believe, if they came to Jesus, said, "Son of David, have mercy on us," and asked to receive their sight. It is no wonder that what stands in the Gospel does not appear in the prophet in the same words. Those who served as ministers of the oracles of the New Testament often did this, as we have noted elsewhere. Still, the words of Isaiah mean the same as those found in the Gospel.

In the present passage we should also note that two things are said about the Savior. The first is the one that also comes first, for believing in him comes first. The second is the one that comes second along the way. This is what lies beyond believing: contemplating the Word, and in contemplating the Word contemplating the Father. Believing extends to the whole multitude of those who come to godliness. But contemplating the Word and perceiving the Father in him no longer extends to all believers, only to the pure in heart. This is how I also understand "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." For whoever directs the sight of his bodily eyes at the body of Jesus has not thereby seen the Father, his God. I think that even [Philip] needed time and training to see Jesus in this way, so that in seeing the Son he might contemplate the Father as well. That is why, when Philip said, "Show us the Father, and that will be enough for us," Jesus said, "Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father." Look into the difference between believing and contemplating, and see whether you can understand the reason behind the two sayings. "And whoever contemplates me contemplates the one who sent me" is not said in the same way as "Whoever believes in me believes not in me but in the one who sent me." Nor [?] is "Whoever believes in me believes not in me but in the one who sent me" phrased like "Whoever contemplates me contemplates the one who sent me." For whoever believes in the Son believes not in the Son but in the Father, the God of the universe. But whoever contemplates the Word, the Wisdom and the Truth contemplates not this alone but also the Father. Before "Whoever believes in me" and "whoever contemplates me" the text says, "Jesus cried out and said." I think this shows how great is the mystery revealed here: first in believing in the Son, and second in contemplating him. For great was the mystical utterance about these things. The evangelist will make clear that it is possible to believe what is contemplated without contemplating it, when he says: "Jesus said to the Jews who had believed in him, 'If you abide in my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.'" Notice carefully that he says "If you abide in my word, you will know the truth" to those who had believed. He speaks to them as people who had not yet come to know the truth but had only believed it.

The true light shone when the Savior of the world came. But they were unwilling to gaze at it or to walk in the radiant splendor of his teachings. As a consequence, darkness overtook them, exacting punishment for the wickedness that already gripped them. And this could fittingly be called being blinded and hardened. Whoever chooses to walk in the light also knows where he is going. In the same way, whoever refuses to walk in the light finds himself walking in darkness and wretchedly traveling the road of the blind and hardened. It was also said earlier that the lightning of the Lord's saving teaching publicly exposed the Jews as blind and hardened. It made the defilement and blindness already in the eyes of their souls more evident and plain. The visible sun, sending down its bright rays, exposes those whose eyes are diseased. So too the intelligible Sun showed the world the light that never sets and knows no evening. Through miracles worthy of God and beyond reason he flashed out the splendor of his divinity, and so exposed all the more the darkness and blindness that already gripped the eyes of the souls of the unfeeling Jews.

Next, because "What shall I say, and what shall I speak?" are joined together, you will ask whether "say" and "speak" differ, or whether they are the same thing stated in parallel. You will therefore set side by side the passages in which "he said" is recorded, and examine them together with those of which "I spoke" is used. Throughout the whole account of creation God is never recorded as "speaking"; instead "he said" is written of him. Consider for yourself whether this contributes anything to the inquiry, in comparison with the phrase repeated continually in Leviticus: "And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying." And see whether you can maintain that "say" signifies an authoritative command, while "he spoke" signifies teaching.

"And I know that his commandment is eternal life." Here one might ask why it does not say that God's commandment procures eternal life, but that it is itself, in its very substance, eternal life. In the same way, knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent is eternal life. Eternal life, then, is each of these. But if God's commandment is eternal life, and God's commandment is in the righteous person who lives blessedly through it, then that life is worth choosing.

This seems to contradict what was said before. Above he speaks as though there were no need to prepare anything, but here he says, "If I go, I will prepare a place for you." What he means, then, is this: as far as the abundance of good things is concerned, which the Father has made ready in his foreknowledge so that those who live well and with all strictness may dwell forever among the good things prepared, there is no need for them to be prepared for you by me; what is needed is for you to show the proper disposition. Nevertheless, I become for you the one who prepares these things and procures them. For what does "I come again and will take you to myself" mean? When, he says, I have given you the means of ascending into heaven and of enjoying the same things, so that the one who has become the cause of these things for you may be made manifest, I myself will come again (he means his second coming from heaven), and taking you I will go up into heaven where I myself am, so as to have you with me, enjoying the same things as I do. "For if we endure," Paul says, "we shall also reign with him."

Thomas seems to have had something precise and carefully examined about him, and this is shown also by what he says. I think he said it not because he disbelieved those who said they had seen the Lord, but because he was wary that it might be a phantom, and remembered the saying, "Many will come in my name, saying, I am he." I think the other apostles also had this experience, but Thomas pre-eminently. [[That the other apostles too had some such thought when they saw Jesus is clear from what is written: "They thought it was a ghost," and he answered and said to them, "Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have bones and flesh as you see that I have."]] As to how it is said to him, "Do not be faithless but believing," and with regard to the name of Thomas, the following might be said. Of those who were to be counted worthy by the Savior of a greater vision—of his transfiguration on the mountain and of Moses and Elijah appearing in glory—he changed the names. The names of the others he did not change, since they were sufficient in themselves to represent the character of each. Concerning the other apostles it is not our task to speak now; but concerning Thomas, which is interpreted Didymus, "Twin," he was so called because he was a kind of twin in his speech, recording divine things in a twofold way, an imitator of Christ, who spoke to those outside in parables but privately explained everything to his own disciples. And it is not absurd to say that the genuine disciples of Christ attain this twofold equipment in speech, which Thomas perhaps already possessed in a special way from that time on. One might also say that the interpretation of this name alone was recorded because the evangelist wished Greeks reading the gospel to take note of the peculiarity of this name's interpretation—the only one interpreted in this special way—so that they might find the reason why his name is also set out in Greek.
Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History VI, 25; see above p. 101, 21–34.
From the second (fifth?) book on John, concerning these same matters:

Origen. Our Savior, therefore, the only-begotten God, who alone was begotten by the Father, is Son by nature and not by adoption. He was born from the very mind of the Father, as will is born from mind. For the divine nature, that is, the nature of the unbegotten Father, is not divisible, so that we should suppose the Son to have been begotten by a division or diminution of his substance. Rather, whether we should speak of God as mind, or heart, or understanding, he remains undivided while bringing forth the offspring of his will, and so became the Father of the Word. And this Word, resting in the bosom of the Father, makes known God, whom no one has ever seen, and reveals the Father, whom no one has known except he alone and those whom the heavenly Father has drawn to him.
Pamphilus, Apology for Origen 5 [IV, 92 Delarue].
On the same matters, in the fifth book on the Gospel according to John:
Origen. The only-begotten Son, our Savior, who alone was born of the Father, is alone Son by nature and not by adoption.
Likewise in the same book:

Origen. There is, then, one true God, who alone has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light; one and true God, so that we may not believe that the name of true God belongs to many. So too those who receive the Spirit of adoption as sons, by which we cry, "Abba, Father," are indeed sons of God, but not as the only-begotten Son is. For the only-begotten is Son by nature, always and inseparably Son; whereas the others, because they have received the Son of God into themselves, have received power to become sons of God. And although they were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God, they were nevertheless not born by that birth by which the only-begotten Son was born. Therefore, as great as the difference is between the true God and those to whom it is said, "I said, You are gods," so great is the difference between the true Son and those who hear, "You are all sons of the Most High."

It would have been more proper to say of God the Word "[?]"; but since he was indicating the existence of the Word in distinction from the incarnation, which took place at a certain time, he used "was" instead of "is." It must be understood that the proper tense meanings of verbs should not be applied to eternal things—that is, "was" and "is" and "will be." For since God the Word is the Son of the Father and is eternal God, the verbs used of him must not be taken as also signifying time, since he himself is not subject to time; and a verb is that which also signifies time, as Aristotle says.

He used appropriate verbs: "became" of the flesh, and "was" of the Godhead. And "through him" is not set down to indicate service but cooperation with the Father, and to show that nothing among existing things is excluded from the making that came about through him.

For the life-giving power in him is able not only to give life but also to fill human souls with knowledge and to drive away ignorance [?]. Paul did not know Christ while he was persecuting him, but when he was illumined by the light of life he recognized the one he was persecuting; and the thief, suffering on the cross, was enlightened and recognized the Life. For the Savior says, "No one can come to me unless the Father draws him."

For the purpose of the one who sent him was that all should believe; and if not all believed and received the illumination, [?] one would not on that account say that it did not rise for this purpose. For the prophets before John became witnesses of the light so that the Hebrews might believe through them. But John, who came after them, bears witness to the Savior's coming so that not only the Hebrews but also all from the Gentiles might believe, as the prophet says: "I will pour out of my Spirit on all flesh"; and David: "All the nations shall serve him."
"Of blood": that is, they have their birth from material things. Indeed, the Savior says to Peter, "Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven."

(Another interpretation:) Those are said to be sons of God who are not "of blood"—that is, not those who offer the sacrifices prescribed by the law, seeking to please God through slaughter and the shedding of blood. "Of the will of the flesh" are those who do everything in order to appear righteous to men; for these have set out to please "by the will of the flesh," circumcising the flesh and wishing to practice Judaism openly, but not caring for the heart and for the Judaism that is in secret. "Of the will of a man" are those who, on the basis of human philosophy, abstain from vice and take up virtue.

In saying "cried out" he means that he proclaimed the coming with boldness and freedom and without any reserve. And the cry refers not to the utterance but to the intensity of the thought. For one who announces great doctrines with the understanding they require proclaims them with a loud voice.
"Has come to be" must be taken in place of "will come to be," for this is the custom of Scripture, as we have said. And "did not overcome" in place of "will not overcome."

For as a prophet and a lamp of light, he trains in advance and accustoms the eye of the soul of anyone who wishes to be enlightened; so too he is the voice of one crying. He calls the Word "the one crying," and John "the voice." A voice must necessarily come before a word, and the task of a voice is to make clear what is signified. And by "wilderness" he means the soul deprived of divine teaching. What does the voice of the one crying command the desert souls? "Make straight the way of the Lord," so as to receive him.

In bearing witness to the light, John knew that he was also God the Word, and the Word is present to every rational being. The thinking faculty [?], which is also called the ruling faculty, is at our very center; for there resides the inner word by which we are rational, which Christ, as God and Word, also watches over—he who was about to come to be baptized. This one, unknown to you, stands in your midst, entering into the hearts and inmost parts of all.

All who were present saw, yet not all believed. But some say that not all of them beheld the Spirit, only John and those who were better disposed. For even if they saw it with their bodily eyes, it was not for that reason entirely evident to all. For the prophets and Moses beheld many other things, and not all the disciples shared in the transfiguration on the mountain, nor did all share in the vision at the resurrection; much less, then, the Jews at the baptism.

It is not possible to see this with the senses, but only with a mind that contemplates the angels coming to minister to Jesus, ascending and descending. "Amen" is found sometimes single and sometimes doubled. The word is Hebrew and means "[?]". For "Amen" is the same as "truly" and "[?]". Many psalms that have "So be it, so be it" at the end have "Amen, Amen" in the Hebrew. It is likely, then, that the Savior, in praying, says, "So be it, so be it, that you may be found faithful, so as to see heaven opened," and the rest of the promise. And "Amen" is also equivalent to "[?]", as in Matthew Jesus says, "Amen I say to you, there are some of those standing here"; but in Luke, "Truly I say to you, there are some of those standing here who will not taste death." That is, "Amen" is equivalent to "[?]", as in "Truly I say to you" that this will happen.

The whip of cords that Jesus made was the sins of the transgressors, by which they were scourged by Jesus and driven out. For Scripture often calls sins cords: "The cords of sinners have entangled me, and their hands weave iniquity together"; and in Proverbs: "Each one is bound tight by the chains of his own sins," that is, he is punished. They were scourged by Jesus and driven out of the temple by the cord they themselves had woven. For the righteous judge could not weave and bring punishment upon the ungodly from any other source than from the things in which they themselves had sinned and transgressed.

It must be said that water differs from Spirit only in concept and not in substance, as the Savior says: "Whoever believes in me, out of his belly will flow rivers of living water." This he said about the Spirit, which those who believed in him were to receive. For if it is said of the Spirit that it flows out like water in rivers, the water will differ from the Spirit only in concept. As, then, one is born of the Savior—wise from Wisdom, true from Truth, and life from Life—since the origin and birth of all is one, so also from the Holy Spirit one is born holy and spiritual, and from the water cleansed. And being watered so as to bear fruit, he is born of water and Spirit.

Matthew spoke of the realm that is ruled, in which these receive their inheritance, while John and Luke named it after God who reigns. For among us too, in ordinary usage, a kingdom is sometimes designated by the one who reigns and sometimes by the place; as we say "the kingdom of the Romans" and "king of Egypt."

For it visits only the earnest, those who have faith and virtue; but from the wicked, who are estranged, it is far away. "Far" and "near" must not be understood spatially, but with reference to whether the vessels receiving its [?] illuminations have been cleansed or not. And "it blows where it wills" shows that the Spirit is a substance; for some think that it is an activity of God, without its own subsistence. That is why the apostle, after enumerating the gifts of the Spirit, added: "All these are worked by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each as he wills." So too what is said in Acts: "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"; and again: "While they were fasting," it says, "and worshiping the Lord, the Holy Spirit said, Set apart for me Paul and Barnabas for the work to which I have called them." And the prophet Agabus says, "Thus says the Holy Spirit: The man who owns this belt they will bind," and so on.

This seems to be said of those who are neither utterly wicked nor perfect in virtue: that, being deceived [?] in both respects, they can be seen to love the darkness rather, since they do its works. For human beings, having free will and being obliged to accept the light and reject the darkness, do the opposite: they accept the darkness and flee the light. That they loved the darkness more must not be understood as a comparison with the light; for they did not love the light at all, since they hated it. That this understanding of the words is correct is clear: those who do evil hate the light, and if they hate the light, they do not love the darkness merely by comparison. Similar is the apostle's saying about wicked people, that they would be "lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God." And in the Psalms: "The wicked one loved evil more than goodness, injustice more than speaking righteousness."

The bride is the human soul, which of itself brings forth nothing good; but if, like a woman, it is receptive by nature to another, it gives birth to virtues both practical and intellectual. The bridegroom, who sows good things in her, is none other than Christ Jesus, to whom I bear witness and whom I baptize. And the friend is the one who stands beside him with firm assent and holds a steadfast faith in him. For none of those who are with Jesus himself is shaken. So also Moses, who lived virtuously, heard God say, "But you, stand here with me"; for God does not stand with us, but we stand with him, as he holds out to us the unshakable standing that comes from him.

Whoever does not have a heavenly mind but is earthly is said to be "of dust" and to bear the image of the man of dust. Therefore, even if he ever professes to have wisdom, it is earthly, unspiritual, demonic, as James the apostle says.

Here again we take the word "love" in a rather human sense. There is a natural law, one toward offspring, and another, of a different kind, toward things loved in other ways. For if God loves righteousness, he loves it as God, as in "I am God, who love righteousness and hate robbery with injustice." For he does not love it as a human being does, so as to possess it within himself and act in accordance with it. The Father loves the Son also as truth, wisdom and sanctification, as David says: "For behold, you have loved truth." And he loves the Son as Father, not as God; but he loves the world as God and as its Creator, not as Father.

One may also speak allegorically: Jacob's well is the teaching of Moses through the law. His sons and his flocks drank from it—the twelve patriarchs and the peoples born from them. But those who drink from this spring thirst again; that is, as time goes on they thirst and come to the saving teaching of the gospel, which no other will succeed. "For heaven and earth will pass away," as the Savior says, "but my words will not pass away."
[For even the mere sight of the one who is envied is apt to kindle no small spark in the envious.]
[For this reason he would have mixed with us [?] . . . . and becoming [?] to the demons.]

He was a beggar because he lacked necessities and was helpless. Such [?] you would find those from among the Greeks and barbarians to be who beg for the benefit and provision of Christ's truth and for the knowledge of his rich teachings. And Jesus freed him not only from blindness but also from begging; for together with sight he granted him what is necessary for the salvation of the soul. Here blindness is the cause of begging, but in Acts it is lameness.
If whoever does not keep the sabbath is not from God, then neither are your priests from God, who profane the sabbath through circumcision.

Having made him trustworthy, they in this way set him up to be shown false [?]. When Christ opened the eyes of the blind man, he did not open those of a little child but of a man of full age, so that he might both see and make his defense as a man. Such also were the other blind men who received their sight.

"You did not listen" means "You were not willing to accept what was said." And "Why then do you want to hear it again?" is equivalent to "If you do not accept what has been said, why do you want it to be told to you again in vain?"

If God does not listen to sinners, how did Christ teach sinners to pray, saying, "Forgive us our trespasses, as we also forgive our debtors"? God listens to those who are turning toward repentance, even if they have not yet stopped sinning. And if God did not listen to sinners, he would not have eaten and drunk with tax collectors and prostitutes. Or else it means that whoever prays about works such as were the works of Jesus, that God may accomplish such things—him God does not hear.

If they took up stones before, they took them up again too. I think that whoever slanders someone is throwing stones at him. They were speaking ill of him, and a division arose among the Jews because of him. So again, having taken up the weight of slanderous words, they threw stones at him. That is why Wisdom says, "Whoever throws a stone on high throws it on his own head"; and the psalmist: "His injustice will come down on his own head." The unjust man who speaks against what is on high is throwing on high.

Just as the day is divided into twelve hours, so the twelve patriarchs and the band of the apostles are equal in number to the hours of the day, having as their sun Christ our God, who is also the spiritual day, from whom come the words and the illumination of the knowledge of them.

And again they sought to kill him, as has often been said. But now they confirmed their resolve and † put it into action [?]. And again he saves himself in a human way, as he constantly does. He gave the reason: that his hour had not yet come. And now he stays near the wilderness in a town called Ephraim. And he remained there with his disciples, waiting for the fitting time and sparing them from destruction.

Whoever follows him serves him, and in this way is his servant. And therefore, where the Word is, there he is also. The promise is not to be understood bodily or spatially. Yet if someone takes it to mean a place, he too would not be wrong. For in the resurrection those who excel in brightness, receiving according to their worth, come to be in the purest regions of the ether, made more translucent by the fineness of light, as places best suited for the leisure of contemplating God the Word.

"One" is said in many ways—by likeness and in many other senses. By agreement, as when it says, "The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul"; by likeness, as when it says, "For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body," that is, by likeness of nature. And just as we, having Adam as the beginning and head of our natural birth, are all said to have one body, so too we enroll Christ as our head through the divine regeneration, which has become for us a figure of his death and resurrection, since he rose as the firstborn from the dead. We enroll him as head as a foreshadowing of his resurrection, "whose members we are individually, and a body, being reborn through the Spirit to incorruption."
